♻ ☆ FastBridge: Closing the Model-Based Realization Gap in Safety Filters on 3D Gaussian Splatting for Fast Quadrotor Flight
Dario Tscholl, Yashwanth Kumar Nakka, Brian Gunter
Fast quadrotor flight requires safe obstacle avoidance under tight onboard compute limits. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides a continuous, geometry-aware scene representation for perception-driven navigation, existing 3DGS safety filters use reduced-order models such as single- and double-integrators that ignore actuator limits and assume commanded accelerations are realized instantaneously. Building on an analytic collision cone barrier for 3DGS, we introduce a nonlinear, actuator-aware safety filter enforced through the full quadrotor dynamics. We derive a high-relative-degree collision cone exponential CBF (ECBF) and a backup CBF whose forward-simulated backup policy provides a certified admissible fallback whenever the QP is infeasible under input constraints. Compared with a state-of-the-art 3DGS safety filter, our approach reduces trajectory jerk by 47% and runs 2.25 times faster. We demonstrate the ECBF in simulation and validate the backup CBF on hardware for real-time navigation in cluttered, perception-derived environments.
comment: preprint, 8 pages, 4 figures
♻ ☆ Learning Options for Compositional Motor Control with Adapter Banks NeurIPS
Sreejan Kumar, Marcelo Mattar, Lea Duncker
Learning flexible motor primitives is a hallmark of skilled motor control. Recent neuroscience theory proposes that motor primitives may be implemented as low-rank perturbations of a shared recurrent network, but leaves open how such a system is learned. We translate this principle into a novel architecture for learning motor skills end-to-end: a shared recurrent core modulated by a bank of residual adapters, each selected by a discrete latent code. Trained on closed-loop biomechanical control, the adapters develop emergent low-rank perturbations of the recurrent dynamics despite no architectural rank constraint, placing task representations in disparate subspaces of the shared core network. A simple high-level policy over the learned options, optimized while the whole network is frozen, sequences the low-rank adapters to produce novel out-of-distribution movements. We demonstrate the ability to generalize to novel motor sequences within the closed-loop control setting, improving on the generalization error of a task-input-conditioned multitask baseline by approximately sevenfold.
comment: Published in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 2026
♻ ☆ Do Latent World Models Really Select the Right Actions?
Zhengshu Zhang, Zhiyuan Li
This paper shows that the planning success of a latent world model does not reveal how well its score selects actions. Latent world models score candidate action sequences by the distance between their predicted embeddings and the embedding of a goal image, and their strong planning results are naturally read as evidence that this score picks good actions. Our study is simple: we take two released models, JEPA-WM and DINO-WM, execute the action sequences their planners consider, and compare what the score prefers with what actually happens. We make two observations. First, the score is informative but unreliable: it picks better actions than chance, yet it often passes over a successful sequence that the search has already found. Second, planning still succeeds, helped by a wider search and by replanning from new observations. With the released search budget, PointMaze planning succeeds in 91% of episodes, yet the top-scored candidate at the end of a search is no more likely to succeed than a random one. These observations suggest that the score should be measured directly, next to the success rate.
comment: 24 pages, 9 figures
♻ ☆ RoboValue: A Fine-Grained Sim-and-Real Benchmark for Unified Evaluation of Robotic Value Models
Shengbang Liu, Zhengye Du, Zhilong Wan, Honghao Su, Chenxiang Xia, Chang Ge, Jinyang Xiao, Nan Wang, Zhipeng Hu, Huining Yuan, Shu'ang Yu, Yue Chen, Tianxing Chen, Chuankang Li, Maoqing Yao, Wenbo Ding, Yu Wang, Guanghui Ren, Chao Yu
Robotic value models assess task execution from visual observations and instructions, providing feedback on execution quality and progress toward the task goal. However, existing evaluations cover only selected aspects of execution understanding, leaving the reliability of value feedback insufficiently tested. We introduce RoboValue, a fine-grained sim-and-real benchmark for unified evaluation of robotic value models. Its framework evaluates four complementary capability dimensions through shared interfaces: task-state understanding, temporal progress monitoring, failure and recovery reasoning, and value consistency. Diagnostic trajectories and instruction variations test whether value judgments accurately reflect task requirements and changes throughout execution. RoboValue-Dataset covers 15 simulation and 20 real-world manipulation tasks, providing expert demonstrations for training and annotated trajectories for fine-grained evaluation. We evaluate representative robotic value models and general-purpose multimodal models in zero-shot and one-shot settings under standard conditions and separate shifts in robot embodiment and environment. Models trained to grade partial outcomes and individual task steps exhibit strong fine-grained grounding, while reasoning over observation histories supports tracking of accumulated task effects. Strong forward-progress and memory scores can nevertheless coexist with poor responses to task regression. Even models with strong grounding and progress estimates struggle to recognize effective recovery and to give consistent feedback within and across valid executions. These findings identify concrete targets for value supervision, while the dataset and public leaderboard support continued assessment of feedback reliability. The website is available at https://robovalue-benchmark.github.io/.
♻ ☆ Off-Policy RL with Online Inference Tuning: 1st Place Solution to the CoRL 2026 RoboEval Challenge
Ilia Larchenko
The CoRL 2026 RoboEval challenge has eight bimanual tasks, and it ranks a policy not only on whether it succeeds but on how: every stage of the task, done safely, efficiently and with both arms in coordination, scored against human demonstrations. My solution has two parts. The generic part, carried over from my LeHome challenge solution, is off-policy RL on a $π_{0.5}$-based policy that is also its own value function. It is trained with AWR and RECAP on advantages of the exact official score, in a loop where every rollout is at the same time a Thompson-sampling trial of about 20 inference parameters. Out of the box, it took the policy to 0.85 RDS on held-out seeds in two days (and it was still very far from convergence). The competition-specific part adds data that local exploration cannot find: generated demonstrations that reach the full reward, and recovery episodes that start from the policy's own failures. The submitted policy reaches 0.990 RDS on my held-out seeds and 0.987 on the official seeds, and it won first place in the challenge, with 0.988 in the organisers' final evaluation on 1,000 unpublished seeds per task.
comment: 1st place solution of the RoboEval Challenge at CoRL 2026. Code: https://github.com/IliaLarchenko/RoboEvalSolution ; checkpoint: https://huggingface.co/IliaLarchenko/RoboEvalSolution ; project page: https://ilialarchenko.com/projects/roboeval2026/
♻ ☆ Concurrent Semantic Search and Mission Execution for LTL Missions in Unknown Environments
Fernando Salanova, David Morilla-Cabello, Cristian Mahulea Poleuca, Eduardo Montijano
Planning complex missions in unknown environments requires robots to reason simultaneously about what they should do and what they still need to discover. Existing approaches for solving LTLf missions typically assume a known environment, or separate the exploration of the environment from the execution of the mission, while semantic exploration methods look for one target at a time and ignore the mission being executed. To fill this gap, our main contribution is an adaptive high-level planning method that interleaves a task-driven semantic search with the execution of the mission, advancing both in a non-myopic manner. Our method leverages two representations built online, a metric-semantic scene graph, built with a Vision Language Model (VLM), that provides the evidence needed to locate the objects the mission refers to, and the deterministic finite automaton (DFA) encoding the mission, that indicates which of them matter at each mission state. At every planning stage, our planner selects the waypoints that are most valuable for both the semantic search and the advancement of the mission, valuing them over the remaining mission stages in order to avoid blocking states. The selected waypoints are then ordered in a single high-level plan, which is recomputed as new information arrives. In photorealistic indoor environments over five mission types, our method completes more missions than the compared approaches while having to cover less of the environment, and it does so with shorter paths and complying with the restrictions imposed by the mission.
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures
♻ ☆ Quantile-Coupled Flow Matching for Distributional Reinforcement Learning NeurIPS 2026
Michael Groom, Victor-Alexandru Darvariu, Lars Kunze, James Wilson, Nick Hawes
Distributional Reinforcement Learning (DRL) models the full return distribution, making it well-suited to uncertainty-aware and risk-sensitive decision-making. Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) critics are increasingly adopted in DRL, offering dense velocity supervision and a natural axis for scaling critic computation. Yet they carry a hidden metric mismatch: the distributional Bellman operator is a contraction in the Wasserstein distance, but CFM critics pair source and Bellman target samples arbitrarily, so their loss does not control the Wasserstein distance to the Bellman target. We show that this mismatch can be fixed with a single sorting operation. Our method, FlowIQN, sorts source and target samples within each mini-batch so that each source quantile is transported to its matching target quantile, approximating the monotone optimal transport coupling. We prove that this quantile coupling makes the CFM loss upper-bound, up to a constant, the squared 2-Wasserstein projection error. To our knowledge, this makes FlowIQN the first flow-matching critic whose training is an approximate Wasserstein projection of the Bellman target, and the guarantee extends to shortcut models for few-step inference. Empirically, the quantile coupling recovers multi-modal returns more accurately than an otherwise identical uncoupled flow with as few as two integration steps. FlowIQN improves substantially on the flow critic Value Flows in a fixed-policy diagnostic and is competitive on offline RL benchmarks across multiple policy extraction methods, identifying the coupling as a central design axis for flow-based critics. Code: https://github.com/ori-goals/flowIQN
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. v2: camera-ready version. 31 pages. Code: https://github.com/ori-goals/flowIQN
♻ ☆ ComVLA: Communication-Aware Split Inference for VLA Models in 6G-Connected Robotics
Boliang Liu, Wint Yi Poe, Jingyun Di, Riccardo Trivisonno, Giuseppe Caire
Connected robotics is an emerging 6G application where mobile robots follow natural-language instructions to manipulate physical objects. The Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that enable this are too large to run on the robot; a common trend is to offload inference to the cloud. The wireless link, however, limits how much sensing data the edge can transmit per control step. Two recent lines address this constraint: semantic communication codecs compress sensor data but require channel-specific retraining, and VLA token pruners select tokens from image but ignore the channel. Our insight is that the dense semantic information contained in the language already indicates which visual tokens matter. We propose ComVLA, a framework that uses this language guidance to adapt the VLA token budget to the channel capacity. Transmitting 32 tokens instead of 512 on the LIBERO benchmark, ComVLA cuts inference compute by 74% and inference latency by 22% versus the original OpenVLA-OFT baseline, at a cost of 1.5 pp in average task success (95.4% vs. 96.9%), and it stays within the capacity budget under Rayleigh and Rician fading. These results demonstrate that co-designing VLA inference and wireless communication is a practical direction for 6G-connected robotics.
comment: 6 pages, accepted to IEEE GLOBECOM 2026
♻ ☆ SuperNav-1.5: Structured Spatial Memory For Agentic Navigation Systems
Jiarui Guo, Jinkai Zhang, Yuanhong Yu, Yongchen Zai, Futang Zhu, Ruizhen Hu, Sida Peng, Xiaowei Zhou
This paper addresses the challenge of scene-level memory design for efficient navigation across sessions and successive object goals. Recent methods commonly represent a scene using scene graphs or image--text records. However, dense scene-graph representations impose substantial reasoning and context overhead on multimodal large language models, while image--text records cannot be directly converted into executable geometric routes. To address these limitations, we propose SuperNav-1.5, an agentic navigation system equipped with a structured spatial memory constructed by the agent. The memory consists of an area-segmented occupancy map annotated with agent-maintained, map-grounded memory nodes. This map guides the agent toward unvisited areas and provides executable routes to known locations. For multi-session navigation, we introduce agent-guided relocalization, whereby the agent infers an area prior from current observations and stored memory records to constrain geometric matching and localize the robot within the stored map. Together, these designs enable efficient navigation across session and successive object goals. Experiments show that our method outperforms baselines on single-object, multi-object, and demand-driven navigation benchmarks, with particularly strong gains in path efficiency. Multi-session evaluation demonstrates that the constructed memory can be reused, while deployment on a real quadruped robot further shows the system's applicability. Project Page: https://zju3dv.github.io/SuperNav-1.5/
comment: 18 pages, 8 figures. Project page: https://zju3dv.github.io/SuperNav-1.5/
♻ ☆ HGeo-TopoMap: Boosting Topological Mapping with Hierarchical Geometric Priors
Siyu Li, Kunyu Peng, Di Wen, Beiping Hou, Zhiyong Li, Kailun Yang
Topological maps provide essential road structure and connectivity information for autonomous driving. However, accurate centerline modeling remains challenging due to the lack of explicit visual markings and the insufficient exploitation of geometric regularities in existing methods. To address these challenges, we propose HGeo-TopoMap, a hierarchical geometric prior learning framework that integrates road-structure guidance and geometric consistency into centerline instance decoding. Specifically, a Geometric Adaptive Learning (GAL) module introduces spatially adaptive cross-attention to incorporate road structure priors derived from inverse perspective mapping, where distance-aware attention biases guide instance queries toward spatially relevant structural information. Furthermore, we develop a hierarchical centerline decoding strategy that progressively predicts instance centers and their constituent points, facilitating the learning of geometric orientations and spatial configurations. Building upon this structured representation, a Geometric Consistency Learning (GCL) module imposes layer-wise contrastive supervision on matched instance queries using geometric groupings, exploiting geometric relationships among centerline instances to regularize instance representations and improve centerline detection. By jointly exploiting spatial structural guidance and instance-level geometric regularities, HGeo-TopoMap enhances centerline detection and topology reasoning. Extensive experiments on the OpenLane-V2 centerline and lane segment benchmarks demonstrate improved topological mapping accuracy. Meanwhile, the proposed method demonstrates stable performance under the robustness benchmark. The source code and model weights will be made publicly available at https://github.com/lynn-yu/HGeo-TopoMap.
comment: The source code and model weights will be made publicly available at https://github.com/lynn-yu/HGeo-TopoMap
♻ ☆ HumanoidPose: Monocular 3D Pose Estimation for Humanoid Robots
Jinlin Gan, Mingzhe Li, Junsheng Zhang, Zhibo Zhou, Jiahan Geng, Yuhua Luo, Changwang Zhang, Chenglu Wen, Lan Xu, Siqi Shen, Cheng Wang
As humanoid robots increasingly enter real-world environments, recovering their 3D whole-body pose from monocular imagery is becoming increasingly important for external state perception, motion analysis, and robot learning. However, Humanoid Robot Pose Estimation (HRPE) lies at the intersection of conventional Robot Pose Estimation (RPE) and Human Pose Estimation (HPE), while not being fully addressed by either paradigm: RPE primarily focuses on non-humanoid robots, particularly fixed-base manipulators, whereas HPE is built upon human-specific skeletal topologies, body models, and motion priors. Despite recent progress in humanoid 2D keypoint detection and HPE adaptation, humanoid-native 3D pose recovery remains insufficiently studied, and a dedicated benchmark with suitable training data and evaluation protocols is still lacking. To address this gap, we introduce Humanoids, a benchmark for monocular 3D humanoid robot pose estimation, and propose HumanoidPose, a framework for this task. Humanoids provides synthetic 3D supervision across diverse humanoid embodiments, manually annotated real-world 2D data, and real-world RGB sequences paired with robot states for 3D evaluation on a physical Roban humanoid. HumanoidPose combines human-inspired visual perception with robot articulation modeling and explicit kinematic grounding. Experiments on Humanoids and the DHRP-H1 benchmark demonstrate strong performance in articulation recovery and 3D pose estimation, including zero-shot transfer to real-world 2D and 3D evaluation. Ablation studies further show the contribution of robot-native articulation modeling and explicit kinematic grounding. The dataset and code will be publicly released to support future research in the community.
♻ ☆ Text-to-CAD Evaluation with CADTests
Dimitrios Mallis, Marco Wang, Ahmet Serdar Karadeniz, Elisa Ricci, Anis Kacem, Djamila Aouada
Text-to-CAD has recently emerged as an important task with the potential to substantially accelerate design workflows. Despite its significance, there has been surprisingly little work on Text-to-CAD evaluation, and assessing CAD model generation performance remains a considerable challenge. In this work, we introduce a new evaluation perspective for Text-to-CAD based on automated testing. We propose CADTestBench, the first test-based benchmark for Text-to-CAD, based on CADTests, executable software tests that verify whether a generated CAD model satisfies the geometric and topological requirements of the input prompt. Using CADTestBench, we conduct comprehensive benchmarking of recent Text-to-CAD methods and further demonstrate that CADTests can also guide CAD model generation, yielding simple baselines that surpass performance of current methods. CADTestBench code and data are available.
♻ ☆ Passive iFIR filters for data-driven velocity control in robotics
Yi Zhang, Zixing Wang, Fulvio Forni
We present a passive, data-driven velocity control method for nonlinear robotic manipulators that achieves better tracking performance than optimized PID with comparable design complexity. Using only three minutes of probing data, a VRFT-based design identifies passive iFIR controllers that (i) preserve closed-loop stability via passivity constraints and (ii) outperform a VRFT-tuned PID baseline on the Franka Research 3 robot in both joint-space and Cartesian-space velocity control, achieving up to a 74.5% reduction in tracking error for the Cartesian velocity tracking experiment with the most demanding reference model. When the robot end-effector dynamics change, the controller can be re-learned from new data, regaining nominal performance. This study bridges learning-based control and stability-guaranteed design: passive iFIR learns from data while retaining passivity-based stability guarantees, unlike many learning-based approaches.
♻ ☆ Localization-Uncertainty-Aware UAV Swarm Search for GNSS-Denied Maritime Surveillance
Siyuan Yang, Junning Lyu, Xiaoyu He, Lakmal Seneviratne, Shaoming He
This paper studies UAV swarm search in GNSS-denied maritime environments, where inter-UAV ranging drives cooperative localization and uncertainty propagates along the multi-hop reference chain, affecting connectivity, collision avoidance, and search effectiveness. We propose a control barrier function (CBF) framework using split covariance intersection (SCI) to fuse neighbor ranges and generate covariance-derived uncertainty scales for mapping and control. Pairwise constraints incorporate inter-step relative displacement to establish continuous-time safe-set invariance across discrete control steps under stated containment, feasibility, and synchronization conditions. A hierarchical Voronoi-target strategy with formation keeping supports efficient forward-looking coverage. Sequential local quadratic programs using preceding-UAV commands complete a 14-UAV search in 221.1 s with 0.45 m root-mean-square localization error while satisfying all separation and reference bounds. Comparisons across search regions, swarm sizes, sampled robust CBF, localizability and formation targets, and model predictive control quantify speed-accuracy-margin trade-offs. Tests on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, a typical UAV onboard computer, verify sub-4 ms mean control cycles and sub-5 ms mean full per-UAV onboard cycles, while Gazebo quadrotor flights verify mission completion and constraint compliance under over-water multipath, beacon-UAV drift, wind turbulence, yaw errors, and communication faults.
comment: 13 pages
♻ ☆ BO-COMM: Bidirectional Optical System for Simultaneous Localization and Communication in Swarm Robotics
Cheng Hu, Haotian Wu, Qi Lin, Manrui Zheng, Shigang Yue, Tao Zou, Jigen Peng
Swarm robotics experiments need to track where robots are, know what state each robot is in, and feed environmental information back to them. Reporting states over a shared radio channel can suffer from contention as the number of robots grows, while static fiducial markers provide pose but cannot report changing states. We present BO-COMM, a bidirectional optical system that observes pose and state through one camera and returns environmental cues through light. Each Colias IV robot, fitted with a CEU-PLUS extension unit, carries a ring of 12 LEDs: a five-bit marker encodes heading, and the remaining seven bits display one of 52 state codes. An overhead camera locates robot centers by ring-based voting and decodes position, heading and state for all visible robots from a single frame. In the downstream direction, a projector renders spatial cues such as virtual pheromone fields, and an infrared channel delivers addressed commands. At 2048x1280 resolution, image-processing time increases only modestly from 2 to 30 robots. Path-following, color-reporting and multi-pheromone experiments show the system closing the loop between optical state reports and projected environmental feedback in a 2.50 x 1.56 m arena.
♻ ☆ Periodic robust robotic rock chop via virtual model control
Yi Zhang, Fumiya Iida, Fulvio Forni
Robotic cutting is a challenging, contact-rich manipulation task where the robot must simultaneously negotiate unknown object mechanics, large contact forces, and precise motion requirements. Our hypothesis is that this complexity can be alleviated through the design of a physically structured virtual-model controller that uses switched virtual mechanisms to generate a robust, rhythmic rock-chop motion for robotic cutting, without requiring pre-planned trajectories or precise environmental information. Motion is generated by the interaction between the environment, the robot's dynamics, and the virtual forces of the switching virtual mechanism, ultimately realized through the available actuation. Through theoretical and numerical analysis, together with experimental validation, we demonstrate that the controlled robot behavior settles into a stable periodic motion. Experiments with a Franka manipulator demonstrate robust cuts across five different vegetables, achieving sub-millimeter slice accuracy for thicknesses from 1 mm to 7 mm at a rate of nearly one cut per second. The controller maintains high performance despite changes in knife shape or cutting board height, and successfully adapts to a different humanoid manipulator, demonstrating robustness and platform independence.
comment: Accepted for publication in The International Journal of Robotics Research
♻ ☆ From Acting to Learning: Experience Selection toward Continually Learning Agents
Yaoyuan Yan, Haoxiang Jie, Zhiyou Heng, Kailin Wang, Yumiao Li, Lifeng Liu, Anwan Yan
We study how selection rules and coverage constraints affect what a 4B language agent learns from successful interactions. The comparison covers nine selectors, two fixed experience pools, eight initialization seeds, and two sampling seeds, producing 288 trained students. Each student is evaluated on 128 development task groups with the same executor. With equal global selection freedom, 256 distinct contents, and 768 training presentations, optimizer-aware gradient selection reaches 81.45\% and 73.19\% success in the two pools. It improves on global random selection by 8.25 and 5.96 percentage points, and on global high-NLL selection by 4.10 and 4.05 points. All eight initialization-level contrasts are positive against both baselines in each pool. Relaxing task/action quotas improves gradient selection but lowers random-selection performance: the benefit of selection freedom depends on the ranking rule. A separately frozen replication on 128 reserved task groups is complete; gradient selection gains +7.03 points over random and +5.03 over high NLL after averaging the two pools equally.
♻ ☆ OmniSLAM: Evidence-Authorized Revision of Persistent Object Maps
Haoxiang Jie, Yaoyuan Yan, Zhiyou Heng, Liang Li, Zhaosong Li, Lifeng Liu
A new surface observation can extend an object map while contradicting an earlier object assignment. Treating both updates as a single merge can join unrelated objects; keeping all earlier assignments leaves fragmented objects unresolved. We present a revision module that makes these decisions separately. Historical merges require shared-mask evidence to outweigh separate-object explanations across views, including after removal of any one observation. New measured points are assigned through local competition among object seeds supported by image masks. On two preselected KITTI-360 windows, the method improves mean building/car instance AP50:90 from 17.259 to 18.762. On four further spatial holdouts, AP rises from 20.263 to 23.171, although unconditional revision reaches 23.251. Controlled comparisons attribute the gains to protecting existing identities, consolidating selected fragments, and assigning new points locally. The results also show where conservative merge decisions suppress useful updates. A garage recording demonstrates the same revision module on LiDAR--inertial--visual mapping outputs.
♻ ☆ ConsisX: Cross-View Consistency Thinking in 3D for Vision-Language-Action Models
Yunhe Zhang, Long Gao, Yuedong Fu, Gang He, Li Xu, Chang Wu, Yuqi Zhu, Pengyu Li
Vision-language-action (VLA) models integrate visual perception and language understanding from vision-language models (VLMs) with action prediction for robotic manipulation. Although multi-view observations provide complementary scene information, VLMs model cross-view interactions based on 2D feature similarity, which can lead to physical inconsistency in the form of cross-view incorrect association between distinct entities and cross-view information fragmentation about the same entity. To address these challenges, we propose ConsisX, a novel VLA framework that integrates cross-view association and entity coherence to enable cross-view consistency thinking in 3D for physically consistent robotic manipulation. Specifically, Cross-View Association Modeling (CAM) is proposed to introduce cross-view spatial proximity constraints in a shared 3D space to reduce cross-view incorrect association. Entity Coherence Organization (ECO) is designed to organize cross-view local information into coherent 3D entity evidence, thereby addressing cross-view information fragmentation. Consistent Action Conditioning (CAC) is introduced to condition action prediction on task-relevant 3D entity evidence for cross-view consistent action execution. Experiments on 3 real-world manipulation tasks and 4 simulation benchmarks establish ConsisX as an effective and competitive framework for robotic manipulation.
♻ ☆ WeaveVLA: 3D Relational Grounding for Vision-Language-Action Models
Zien Wang, Yuhao Pan, Yunfeng Fan, Nan Cheng, Xin Xia, Wenchao Xu
Vision-language-action (VLA) models leverage pretrained vision-language representations for instruction-conditioned robot control, yet their understanding of task-relevant 3D relations and how these relations evolve during manipulation remains largely implicit. To address this challenge, we introduce WeaveVLA, a framework that enhances VLA action generation by explicitly modeling task-relevant relative 3D relations and maintaining relational context across observations. WeaveVLA employs a task-conditioned sparse graph neural network to encode relative 3D relations among objects, the gripper, and nearby references. Pair-specific recurrent edge states integrate geometric evidence across observations to maintain evolving spatial context. A learned-query readout summarizes the updated graph representations into compact relational tokens, which condition the action expert alongside the original vision-language context. An auxiliary geometry reconstruction objective further encourages spatial structure preservation. We instantiate WeaveVLA on StarVLA-GR00T and $π_{0.5}$, achieving over 98% average success on LIBERO with both backbones. On LIBERO-Plus, WeaveVLA improves success from 74.9% to 82.0% and from 85.7% to 87.8%, respectively, with additional improvements on CALVIN D$\rightarrow$D. On three real-world tasks, the StarVLA-GR00T-based variant improves average success from 55.6% to 70.0% under standard conditions and from 33.3% to 53.3% under OOD perturbations, surpassing the $π_{0.5}$ baseline in both settings.
comment: 21 pages, 7 figures
♻ ☆ FluentAct: Efficient Action Continuations for Asynchronous Vision-Language-Action Control
Shuo Bao, Ming Shang, Yuchen Huang, Hongjin Niu, Han Yu, Yilong Qiu, Yifan Wang, Shuo Tian, Jiangtao Wang, Hongyu Wang, Xinzhou Wang, Fuchun Sun
Asynchronous vision-language-action (VLA) policies generate new action chunks while robots continue executing committed commands. Because the robot moves during inference, a chunk generated from an earlier observation can introduce abrupt command changes at handoff. To address this problem, we introduce FluentAct, a framework for efficient action continuation that improves command continuity at handoff. Instruction-aware history and retrieved memory provide task context, while a latent rollout of committed actions constructs the handoff context. An ordered Haar generator predicts pairwise averages and conditional differences with two forward evaluations of a shared action expert. During offline training, a frozen reference samples candidates under the same request and committed prefix. We rank these candidates by command continuity and train the policy with a reference-relative flow-energy objective. The trained policy generates continuations directly without online candidate ranking. FluentAct improves task completion over BehaviorVLA on CALVIN, RoboTwin 2.0 Hard, and six real-world manipulation tasks, achieving a CALVIN average sequence length of 4.52. On LIBERO, it achieves 99.1% success and reduces handoff command jump and trend mismatch by 21.3% and 20.7%, respectively, relative to the variant without preference training. In a separate timing study in unpaced LIBERO simulation on an RTX 4090, its median request-to-handoff latency is 153 ms, 32.5% lower than native $π_{0.5}$.
♻ ☆ Robo-Harness K1: Harnessing Robot-Use Agents via Perception Augmentation
Zexi Li, Yehang Zhang, Wenqian Li, Haojian Huang, Chenxu Wang, Chunyang Zhang, Shiyuan Deng, Yangkai Wei, Tianyi Zhang, Ruize Gao, Binghui Xie, Bohan Zhou, Jinghao Li, Kaiwen Zhou, Yifan Chang, James Cheng, Yinchuan Li
Vision-language models (VLMs) understand manipulation scenes and instructions, yet as robot-use agents they struggle to turn 2D observations into the 3D relations that motion requires. We introduce Robo-Harness K1, a robot-use agent harness built on perception as tools. K1 offers region grounding, calibrated depth and geometry, persistent visual anchors, and projected grasp candidates as callable tools. The VLM calls them to measure the scene, chooses its next motion from the results, and measures again after it acts. On LIBERO-PRO, K1 raises Gemini 3.7 Flash from 16.7% to 71.7% and GPT-6 Astra from 63.3% to 93.3%, with the largest gains on spatial tasks. Without fine-tuning, the Gemini agent transfers to three RoboSuite arms, dual-arm RoboTwin tasks, and mobile manipulation in RoboCasa. In real-world experiments on a Piper arm, K1 completes eight of nine concluded trials across three tasks. Agentic post-training further distills a frontier model's traces into a compact agent: trained on 107 successful episodes, Qwen3.5-9B reaches 44.2% on new initial states and 13.9% on held-out task conditions, versus 30.2% and 0.0% for OpenVLA trained on the same episodes. Mixed training on traces from four environments raises held-out accuracy from 11.1% to 27.8% and RoboSuite success from 28.3% to 50.0%. These results support perceptual tool use for deploying and training robot-use agents.
comment: preprint v2
♻ ☆ YUBI-STAG: Contact and Semantic-Rich Alignment for VLAs via Automated Video-Language Grounding
Masatoshi Tateno, Takehiko Ohkawa, Yueh-Hua Wu, Hanlong Li, Tatsuya Matsushima, Yoichi Sato, Kei Ota
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models acquire broad manipulation capabilities via large-scale pretraining, yet eliciting them through language requires fine-grained alignment between instructions and physical interactions. Existing robot demonstrations typically provide only coarse task descriptions, omitting how actions are executed, including which gripper acts, which object is contacted, and how it is grasped and moved. We introduce YUBI-STAG, a framework for Spatio-Temporal Annotation and Grounding that automatically enriches manipulation demonstrations with interaction-rich semantics to align pretrained VLAs with fine-grained manipulation language. Combining contact-object segmentation with vision-language models, YUBI-STAG annotates object identities, attributes and states, per-gripper actions, bimanual coordination, and spatially grounded interactions. To address YUBI-STAG's reliance on localized sequences and multi-stage VLM inference, we distill it into YUBI-VLM. YUBI-VLM directly recovers action structure and annotations from raw, unsegmented video in few inference calls and operates from wrist views alone. We evaluate both frameworks on YUBI-STAG-Bench across temporal, semantic, and spatial grounding tasks. YUBI-VLM retains much of YUBI-STAG's annotation accuracy with fewer inference calls and shorter runtime while generalizing to unseen manipulations. Finally, post-training VLA policies on these annotations aligns them with fine-grained language and contact-aware structure. Bimanual experiments demonstrate improved performance and instruction following, including control over object identity, acting gripper, target location, and spatial relations absent from original labels.

♻ ☆ SparQ4D: Learning to Act through Sparse 4D Queries
Siyuan Xie, Jinxi Xiao, Ran Ji, Yikai Liu, Mingxi Li, Xuebing Li, Ye Shi, Yuxiang Gao, Jiayuan Gu
Successful manipulation requires a policy to understand where things are and how they will move, yet action demonstrations leave this spatiotemporal structure implicit. While explicit 4D supervision has proven effective, reducing the cost of dense 4D prediction remains challenging. This paper introduces SparQ4D, a lightweight yet expressive decoder that efficiently injects holistic 4D scene understanding into policies and improves success rates. At its core is a query-based decoder attached to a pretrained policy, which casts many spatialtemporal tasks into one unified interface (e.g. depth, 2D/3D point motion, multi-view correspondence, and hand-eye relations). This design enables efficient training and inference without sacrificing expressivity: the policy learns rich 4D structure from a small number of sampled queries during training, while the decoder can be removed at inference with zero additional overhead. Across multiple backbones, simulated environments, and real-world settings, SparQ4D achieves state-of-the-art manipulation performance, outperforming competing methods while training up to $5\times$ faster. Probing analyses further reveal that this 4D structure is recoverable from the policy.
♻ ☆ RoboPace: Contact-Aware Time-Optimal Retiming for Action-Chunk Policies
Mimo Shirasaka, Takehiko Ohkawa, Takuya Okubo, Nicola Scianca, Tatsuya Matsushima, Kei Ota
Robot manipulation data collection has been shifting from teleoperation toward robot-free demonstrations, through interfaces such as the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) or directly from human hands. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies trained on such data inherit the demonstrator's timing. Yet human timing does not directly transfer to robots: compliant hands tolerate fast contact, whereas robots may overshoot due to actuator and tracking limitations; conversely, robots can move faster in free space. This motivates a unified approach that reconciles execution speed with contact safety. We present RoboPace, an online retiming layer that preserves the policy's geometric path while adapting its timing, respecting the target robot's kinematic and dynamic constraints. It adapts execution speed based on predicted contact, jointly accounting for contact-dependent speed limits and the robot's motion constraints. The method requires no policy retraining and operates in real time. Across three contact-rich tasks on a dual-arm robot, faster uniform execution and physical-limit-only retiming largely fail. RoboPace instead achieves higher overall success than slow uniform execution while completing four of five commands in approximately half the time, retaining the reliability of slow execution without its time cost.
comment: Project: https://research.airoa.io/publications/robopace/
♻ ☆ Policy-intrinsic Demonstration Curation
Sunjae Jeong, Geunhyeok Yu, Dowoon Lee, Hyoseok Hwang
Fine-tuning a robot policy for a new target task requires target demonstrations, but only a few are available. Demonstrations of other tasks can fill this gap, and demonstration curation selects the useful ones among these candidates. Retrieval-based curation selects the candidates that are most similar to the target demonstrations. Since it does not use the policy, any candidate that looks similar receives a high score. Performance-aware curation therefore estimates the effect of each candidate on the policy. However, this requires training on the candidates and takes a long time. We propose a third branch, policy-intrinsic curation, which uses the policy and still takes little time. It estimates this effect with forward passes of the pretrained policy and needs no training. We instantiate this branch with PICKER (Policy-Intrinsic Curation from Known Errors). It selects the candidates on which the policy makes errors that agree with those on the target demonstrations. PICKER reaches success rates comparable to those of performance-aware curation and takes about as long as retrieval-based curation. Its selection is also stable across seeds.
comment: 15 pages (including 1 page of references and 6 pages of appendices), 5 figures, 7 tables
♻ ☆ Follow-Bench: A Unified Motion Planning Benchmark for Socially-Aware Robot Person Following
Hanjing Ye, Weixi Situ, Jianwei Peng, Yu Zhan, Bingyi Xia, Kuanqi Cai, Hong Zhang
Robot person following (RPF)---mobile robots that follow and assist a specific person---has emerging applications in personal assistance, security patrols, eldercare, and logistics. To be effective, such robots must follow the target while ensuring safety and comfort for both the target and surrounding people. In this work, we present the first comprehensive study of RPF, which (i) surveys representative scenarios, motion-planning methods, and evaluation metrics with a focus on safety and comfort; (ii) introduces Follow-Bench, a unified benchmark simulating diverse scenarios, including various target trajectory patterns, crowd dynamics, and environmental layouts; and (iii) re-implements eight representative RPF planners, ensuring that both safety and comfort are systematically considered. Extensive simulation experiments provide a quantitative study of safety- and comfort-related physical indicators, while real-world trials of two MPC-based implementations on a differential-drive robot illustrate deployment feasibility and practical following behaviors. These results reveal open challenges and future research directions.
comment: Accepted by T-ASE 2026. Project page: https://follow-bench.github.io/

☆ OmniAct: One Policy, One Million Embodiments
Xiang Fan, Yuheng Wang, Jiayuan Yan, Bohan Fang, Wisdom Oluchi Ikezogwo, Ainaz Eftekhar, Max Argus, Jason Ren, Jiafei Duan, Ranjay Krishna
A single policy that controls diverse robots must not only transfer task knowledge across embodiments, but also adapt its behavior to each robot's capabilities. Existing approaches facilitate transfer through shared action representations, but these representations do not necessarily capture how differences in robot morphology should shape manipulation strategies. We introduce OmniAct, a cross-embodiment manipulation policy that conditions directly on each robot's kinematics in a specific scene to produce embodiment-specific behavior. This kinematic graph represents the robot's joint positions, motion axes, and connectivity to its visual observation, allowing the policy to account for how its embodiment related to objects and surfaces in the scene. A flow-matching policy predicts relative joint motions for each node, enabling control across robots with different degrees of freedom and kinematic configurations. To learn how physical structure shapes behavior at scale, we procedurally design and filter one million physically feasible robot embodiments; next, we develop algorithms to generate robot trajectories in simulation for all embodiments; finally, we train across diverse simulated manipulation tasks. On 2,000 embodiment-scene-held-out evaluation episodes, OmniAct achieves 63.0% success, compared to 17.8% for pi 0.5 and 57.9% for the strongest baseline; on the task families GPT-6 Astra was evaluated on, it achieves 64.7% against GPT-6 Astra's 41.1%. On a previously unseen real-world robot, it achieves nearly twice the success rate of the next best method, MolmoAct2. Beyond task success, we observe that OmniAct learns distinct manipulation strategies that exploit the capabilities and accommodate the limitations of different morphologies. Project: https://omniact.github.io/
☆ PointX: Multi-View Consistent Intrinsics by Querying Surface Points
Miguel Farinha, Sam Sartor, Iliyan Georgiev, Giuseppe Vecchio, Ronald Clark, Michael Fischer
The appearance of a scene is determined by the albedo, roughness, metallicity and normal of every point on its surface, and by the light that reaches it, its irradiance. Recovering these intrinsics from images is ambiguous, and methods that predict them per pixel give the same surface point a different decomposition in every view. We introduce PointX, a simple feed-forward model that predicts intrinsics per 3D surface point instead. A multi-view transformer encodes a set of unposed images, and for any queried surface point, PointX pools the point's tokens across the views in which it appears and decodes the point's intrinsics once. Each point of a 3D reconstruction of the scene, such as a point cloud or a mesh, thus receives a single prediction, which is exactly consistent across views by construction and enables view-consistent relighting and editing. The same model also predicts per-view maps, from one image or many, by querying the point seen at every pixel. These maps agree across views up to the precision of the estimated geometry and correspondences. PointX is significantly more consistent than existing methods, while remaining competitive in accuracy from a single image and improving as views are added. Project page: https://pointx-paper.github.io/

☆ DiaCap: Jointly Learning Who Speaks When for Audiovisual Dialogue Captioning
Binfei Ji, Zhiwen Cao, Anqi Yang, Prem Seetharaman, Shuo Yang, Ratheesh Kalarot, Yingyan Celine Lin, Mingze Xu
We present DiaCap, an audiovisual LLM for comprehensive dialogue captioning, which produces the transcript, timestamps, and a visual description of the speaker for every utterance in a video. Considering that utterance timing and audiovisual diarization are tightly coupled, DiaCap unifies the tasks in a single model, trained in two complementary stages. First, we train DiaCap on 225K curated clips, using synthetic captions that densely label every utterance in detail. Second, we further refine the model via reinforcement learning on 2.9K human-corrected clips, using fine-grained feedback that directly evaluates utterance timing, speaker grouping, and speaker binding. On DiaDemBench, which we extend with utterance-level timestamps and subtitle redaction, both DiaCap with off-the-shelf transcripts and its end-to-end variant DiaCap-E2E achieve strong results. Specifically, DiaCap performs on par with Gemini 4 Argon in audiovisual diarization while clearly outperforming it in timestamp accuracy (76.59 vs. 42.76 TIME). It also maintains strong diarization on multilingual and minute-long videos, and transfers to audiovisual question answering.
comment: 18 pages, 13 figures, 12 tables
☆ BioLoom: Scaling Biomedical Vision-Language Models by Learning from the Structure of Scientific Articles
Yuwei Yang, Xiaoxiao Sun, Alejandro Lozano, Yuan-Sen Ting, Yuhui Yuan, Liang Zheng, Serena Yeung-Levy
The development of biomedical vision-language models (VLMs) with contrastive image-text pretraining has been driven by scaling to increasingly large and diverse image-text datasets. Beyond scaling, further progress can come from learning richer representations from existing data. We hypothesize that the structure of scientific literature itself provides an additional source of supervision: figures, panels, captions, and accompanying article text encode rich relationships across modalities. Yet, treating these as independent image-text pairs overlooks their relationships. To address this limitation, we incorporate these structural relationships into contrastive image-text supervision. We preserve exact image-text matches while introducing weaker positive supervision for related pairs, such as a panel and the caption of a sibling panel. We upweight cross-article negatives of the same content type to encourage finer discrimination. We also enrich panel descriptions using visual content, original figure captions, and mentioning paragraphs. Pairing panels with these descriptions and whole figures with their original captions yields Loom52M, a dataset of 52.4 million image-text pairs spanning scientific charts and biomedical images. Using Loom52M, BioLoom (DFN-2B) achieves 56.82% domain-balanced mean accuracy across 67 zero-shot classification tasks from 43 datasets in 10 domains, compared with 48.77% for MedPMC-CLIP. On BioLoomBench with concise captions and BioMedFlickr, it achieves bidirectional mean Recall@1 of 63.20% and 10.59%, versus 46.37% and 7.55% for the respective strongest evaluated baselines, BiomedCLIP and MedPMC-CLIP. Code, datasets, benchmarks, and models are available at https://bioloom-clip.github.io/.

☆ One Take, Many Cameras: Audio-Grounded Shot Synthesis for Dialogue Re-Cinematography
Anthony Chen, Naomi Ken Korem, Matan Ben-Yosef, Tavi Halperin, Urska Jelercic, Ofir Bibi, Daniel Cohen-Or, Or Patashnik, Maneesh Agrawala
Creating a dialogue scene typically requires cutting between multiple views (e.g., close-ups, medium shots, and over-the-shoulder shots) of the actors. Yet capturing such coverage is costly and in many settings unavailable. We study dialogue re-cinematography: synthesizing additional shots from a single wide-angle dialogue video. Existing video generators can synthesize new shots, but rely on visual cues alone, so when the source video barely shows the lips, the generated lip motion fails to match the speech. Our key observation is that the speech audio is view-invariant: it constrains lip motion in any target view. Building on this insight, we adapt a pretrained audio-visual diffusion model to generate the new shot from a target frame that specifies the view, a source video that contains the performance, and the speech audio that drives lip motion. In multi-person scenes, however, pretrained audio-visual models drive every visible face with the same speech, causing speech leakage, where silent listeners mouth the speaker's words. We therefore introduce speaker-aware audio gating, a training-free module that lets the audio drive only the faces that speak in the target shot. On a cinematic paired-view benchmark spanning diverse viewpoints and framings, our method lowers perceptual error by 59%, landmark error by 56%, and speech leakage by 97% relative to the strongest baseline, Wan 3.0. Our method also remains robust on in-the-wild scenes, highlighting its potential for film post-production.
comment: Project page: https://recinematography.github.io/
☆ Lost on Campus: Evaluating Embodied Spatial Reasoning of Vision-Language Models in the Wild NeurIPS 2026
Zehan Zheng, Yanyuan Chen, Deming Li, Yutao Tang, Jianwen Xie, Alan Yuille, Jieneng Chen, Cheng Peng
Embodied Spatial Reasoning (ESR) is central to deploying Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in real-world embodied tasks, yet remains inadequately evaluated. Existing benchmarks primarily assess spatial reasoning in static images or synthetic indoor environments, where semantic shortcuts often suffice, making it difficult to faithfully evaluate spatial reasoning capabilities in the wild. In light of this, we present Lost on Campus, a benchmark for evaluating ESR in large-scale real-world outdoor 3D environments reconstructed by 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our benchmark introduces a unified reasoning-action evaluation framework that seamlessly integrates diagnostic QA for isolated reasoning with closed-loop interactive navigation for active reasoning under multimodal instructions. To enable fine-grained diagnosis, we evaluate six capability aspects of ESR: action grounding, spatial foresight, metric awareness, goal-directed planning, ego-allocentric localization, and spatio-temporal consistency. Extensive experiments reveal that: (i) Compared to indoor settings, real-world outdoor environments impose substantially higher demands on spatial reasoning, where existing models exhibit poor performance; (ii) VLMs still struggle with fine-grained visual alignment, with failures in spatial foresight and ego-allocentric localization emerging as primary bottlenecks; (iii) Improving multimodal interaction capabilities and long-term spatial reasoning is crucial for advancing embodied intelligence. These findings highlight that faithful evaluation of ESR demands benchmarks tightly coupling perception, reasoning and action within realistic and continuous environments.
comment: NeurIPS 2026. Project page: https://dyfcalid.github.io/Lost-on-Campus/
☆ ROAM-Bench: Evaluating Embodied Active Spatial Intelligence through Evidence Verification
Xingjian Ran, Xiaoye Mo, Sihao Liu, Li Luo, Taiqiang Wu, Ji Zhao, Wenqi Shao, Hongyang Li, Jiaqi Wang, Bo Dai
Embodied spatial intelligence requires agents to gather information through exploration and interaction, then use it to reason and act. Existing benchmarks insufficiently distinguish correct outcomes from completion of these task requirements. We introduce ROAM-Bench to evaluate these abilities under robot motion and collision constraints. Independent checks use simulation state and episode records to assess outcomes and task requirements, with stronger checks of geometry, coverage, or placement. It comprises 250 manually validated tasks across 11 types in five groups and 27 indoor environments, covering object and room search, counting, geometric judgments, direction reasoning, and relocation. Human evaluators achieve 84% strict task success on 100 sampled tasks, with every correct outcome satisfying the required checks. Across seven frontier vision-language models, we identify two complementary failure modes: correct outcomes with unmet task requirements, and incorrect outcomes despite passing stronger checks. Oracle-input diagnostics show that more complete target observations and calibrated feedback improve final spatial judgments.

☆ iWAM: Efficient Action Prediction from World Models without Explicit Future Prediction
Vansh Kapoor, Max Sobol Mark, Sreyas Venkataraman, Max Simchowitz, Aviral Kumar
World-action models (WAMs) build policies on pretrained video-generation models, on the premise that predicting how a scene evolves helps determine how to act. However, generating future scenes is expensive for real-time control. This motivates efficient proxies for future imagination, but how to train such proxies without sacrificing action-prediction quality remains unclear. An effective proxy need not generate a high-resolution frame; it only needs to provide enough information to distinguish between possible futures. This leads to the design principle behind iWAM: rather than denoising an entire future frame, can we condition the action policy on intermediate features from a single video-model evaluation? We show that the answer is yes. Exploiting the reversible dynamics of flow-matching models, we invert each training future into the corresponding latent noise vector. However, a single velocity evaluation at this latent does not necessarily yield informative features for action prediction. We therefore learn a bidirectional flow map that amortizes future-generation computation, enabling a single model evaluation to provide effective conditioning features. At inference, we sample a latent noise vector from the prior and condition the policy using just one video-backbone forward pass. Across simulated benchmarks and real robots, iWAM recovers the generalization benefits of WAMs while substantially reducing its inference cost.
☆ Physicl Scenes: An Artist-created 3D Dataset for Learning Perception and Action
Yueh-Cheng Liu, Snehal Jauhri, Matthias Nießner, Angela Dai
We present Physicl Scenes, a high-quality artist-created and curated dataset of 6,499 3D scenes spanning household rooms, public interiors, and outdoor spaces. The dataset combines detailed geometry, physically based materials, and carefully composed environments with object- and part-level semantic annotations, providing rich, joint supervision for visual and embodied learning. We demonstrate its value as training data across inverse rendering, 3D reconstruction, scene understanding, and mobile manipulation. Across these tasks, training state-of-the-art methods with our scenes improves performance over alternative synthetic datasets. In addition, we introduce a mobile manipulation benchmark, evaluating vision-language-action models performing physical pick and place in diverse 3D scenes with realistic layouts, and using our part annotations to also score where each object is grasped. Our dataset will be released publicly to facilitate research in visual and embodied AI.

☆ BriConstrain: Geometrically Constrained Decoding for Autoregressive Brick Assembly Generation
Nadav Magar, Amir Hertz, Ariel Shamir, Or Patashnik
Language models can generate LEGO$^\circledR$ assemblies from text, but their builds often contain parts that collide or attach to nothing. The usual approach of rejecting and resampling invalid placements discards decoded tokens without guaranteeing a valid build. We present BriConstrain, a constrained decoding method that restricts a pretrained language model's next-token probabilities before sampling, steering it towards valid placements. Because the validity of a brick placement depends on the non-predetermined build state, it cannot be compiled into a fixed grammar and must be checked dynamically. However, checking the validity of a brick before sampling is challenging as the space of valid placements is combinatorially large and cannot be enumerated exhaustively. Our key idea is to narrow the search space by constraining how parts attach rather than which parts attach to each other. Concretely, given the model's predictions of the currently placed part, and the previously placed parent it wants to connect to, we constrain the model's choice of how they attach. This allows us to span the space of part attachments, using a precomputed geometric oracle, and to effectively filter out colliding options. With valid attachment candidates in hand, we bias the model's next-token distribution towards the remaining valid candidates. We evaluate our method on two LEGO$^\circledR$ formats and models: BrickNet, which annotates connectivity explicitly, and our proposed Implicit Connectivity LDraw Format (ICLF), which uses numeric values for placements and leaves connectivity implicit. Our method raises collision-free builds from 31% to 91% on BrickNet and from 15% to 65% on ICLF, and outperforms rejection sampling on both formats at about 60% of its decoding cost.

☆ Read My Lips: Context-aware Lip Reading Using Language and Audio-Visual Models
Amir Razlighi, Zhuo Ning, Naomi Ken Korem, Nisarg Patel, Yiorgos Chrysanthou, Daniel Cohen-Or, Ali Mahdavi Amiri
Real-world speech is often partially observable: audio may be missing or corrupted by noise and competing speakers, while the speaker's lips remain visible. Recovering speech requires combining what can be heard, seen, and inferred from context. We introduce RML (Read My Lips), a collaborative method combining a lip reader, a language model, and an audio-visual generative model. The lip reader provides articulation hypotheses, the language model uses context to resolve ambiguous or missing words, and the audio-visual generator reconstructs synchronized speech while preserving speaker identity. Since source reliability varies, RML generates multiple reconstructions and uses the available evidence to favor the most reliable ones. This allows RML to handle missing audio, strong interference, and poor visual evidence without manually defined thresholds. Quantitative and qualitative experiments across these conditions show the benefit of combining visual, acoustic, and linguistic signals.

☆ EventDiffusion: Learning Native Event Stream Distribution from Videos
Karthik Sundar Senthilkumar, Christopher Thirgood, Simon Hadfield
Event cameras capture asynchronous brightness changes at high temporal resolution, but scarce recordings constrain data-driven research. Sparse RGB observations cannot uniquely determine intervening events since identical frames may correspond to streams with different activity, polarities, and timing. Existing simulators largely rely on prescribed sensor dynamics and estimated brightness trajectories, whose assumptions limit the diversity and fidelity of plausible event streams. We introduce EventDiffusion, a hierarchical generative framework that directly learns the conditional distribution of native asynchronous event streams from real recordings. EventDiffusion decomposes generation into three probabilistic processes: Event Activity Diffusion (EAD) learns stochastic discrete event counts; Event Spatial Allocation (ESA) distributes these counts to individual pixels while preserving cardinality; and Event Timing Diffusion (ETD) learns continuous asynchronous timestamp distributions. We also introduce CEFS, an event-stream realism metric combining event activity and polarity with multiscale space-time structure and temporal fidelity. Across all datasets, EventDiffusion achieves double the accuracy of SOTA methods and demonstrates robustness across different cameras at any resolution.

☆ The Radar-based Activities of Daily Living (R-ADL) Dataset
Dominique Regli, Brian C. Williams
Monitoring Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) supports safety and well-being for people living at home, especially older adults, and radar sensing is gaining increasing attention in the field of activity recognition for its ability to ensure privacy in the home while also surpassing technical limitations of other sensing modalities. However, radar-based activity recognition remains constrained by the limited availability of large-scale datasets. We introduce the Radar-based Activities of Daily Living (R-ADL) dataset to addresses the gaps identified in existing work: 1) it expands the scale of available data by providing over eight hours of annotated recordings in which a person performs eight distinct activities; 2) it overcomes room configuration limitations by recording from five different locations in a two-bedroom, two-bathroom apartment; and 3) it extends beyond primitive actions to focus on high-level ADLs. In addition to the dataset, this paper introduces practical guidance for future ADL dataset construction. We conducted a detailed analysis of how ADLs are prioritized across academic research, health survey tools, and clinical trials to identify clinically significant ADLs. Furthermore, we provide our experimental design, data collection and annotation strategies, post-processing pipeline for forming the R-ADL dataset from raw data, and baseline results on standard machine learning architectures. The R-ADL dataset serves as a valuable resource for advancing ADL recognition systems as we continue building larger and more diverse datasets.
☆ SUPRA: Synthesizing Amyloid PET from MRI and Plasma Biomarkers with an Explicit Regional SUVR Prior
Hanwen Li, Fadi Deek, Zhi Wei, Ruixiang Tang, Feng Liu, Bharat Biswal, Michal Schnaider Beeri, Auriel Willette, Chenxi Yuan
Amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) quantifies brain amyloid-$β$ as a standardized uptake value ratio (SUVR), but is costly and not widely available. Structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is routine, and plasma biomarkers such as phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) are becoming practical. Synthesizing amyloid PET from MRI alone is ill-posed, because brain anatomy reveals little about amyloid burden. We present SUPRA (SUVR prior-guided amyloid synthesis), which divides this task between MRI and plasma biomarkers. A regression maps the plasma panel to regional SUVR levels, painted onto the subject's MRI segmentation as an explicit prior. A 3D network then adds a residual correction guided by MRI. The output is in absolute SUVR, and the model also runs on p-tau217 alone. On the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort (111 test pairs), SUPRA reaches a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 23.4 dB, against at most 20.7 dB for four published models, and rank correlations of 0.56 to 0.67 with true SUVR in the composite cortex, an early-accumulation region and the striatum, against at most 0.24. In a second, cognitively unimpaired cohort with other plasma platforms (143 test pairs), it reaches 22.8 dB and 0.32 to 0.61, against at most 21.4 dB and 0.20. Its area under the curve for amyloid positivity is 0.91 and 0.82, against at most 0.63. Ablations show that plasma supplies the amyloid information and the network the image quality. Combining MRI with a blood test yields synthetic amyloid PET that is realistic and tracks burden across regions.

☆ Spectrify: Framework for Hyperspectral Image Generation Using Computer Graphics
Yasin Mamedov, Daniil Vladimirov, Sofiia Dorogova, Bakhtiyar Khalfin, Egor Ershov
Hyperspectral images (HSIs) record the full spectrum of light at every pixel, so projecting an HSI through a camera's spectral sensitivities gives that camera's RAW image, and one HSI can supply training data for hyperspectral reconstruction and camera-pipeline methods. Real HSIs, however, are slow and expensive to capture, and the largest datasets hold only about 1,000 images. High-level vision commonly replaces scarce real data with images rendered from 3D scenes. Low-level tasks, however, need physically correct spectra, which requires spectral rendering with a measured spectrum for every material in a scene, and existing spectral renderings cover only a handful of scenes, mostly with a simplified image formation model. We present Spectrify, a framework that converts 3D scene datasets into HSIs, together with a library of reflectance spectra labeled by material and compiled from close-range hyperspectral datasets and spectrophotometer measurements. In Spectrify, spectra follow the material: each object receives a physically based optical model and measured reflectance spectra or optical constants from its material category, each lamp an emission spectrum of its type and the sky a modeled daylight spectrum, and Mitsuba 3 path-traces the full light transport of each scene per wavelength. We show that a hyperspectral reconstruction network trained only on our synthetic HSIs generalizes to unseen real datasets better than networks trained on the largest real HSI datasets on most test sets, and that assigning spectra by material category instead of by color alone improves this transfer on every test set. RAW images projected from our HSIs are also useful training data for color constancy, performing on par with existing synthetic RAW generators. We release the 4,500 rendered HSIs, the code of Spectrify and its material-labeled reflectance library.
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables; includes supplementary material
☆ Linear Probes Can Guide: Training-Free Control of Representation Generators
Pengwei Wang, José Morano, Botond Fazekas, Hrvoje Bogunović
Representation-space generative models, such as Representation Autoencoders (RAEs), leverage pretrained vision foundation models (VFMs) primarily to accelerate training and improve sample fidelity. Yet VFMs are more than reconstruction tokenizers, as they feature rich representation spaces that are highly organized and linearly readable. We observe that this removes a key obstacle of post-hoc guidance: by linearity of expectation, a clean probe applied to an ideal denoiser's prediction yields the exact posterior mean of the probe scores at any noise level. This regime, which we call Semantic Mean-Space, turns semantic guidance into a Bayesian linear inverse problem, bypassing the need for training-time conditioning. With this foundation, we propose LiSM, a unified framework for Linear Guidance in Semantic Mean-Space. To validate the framework, we developed and adapted different solvers, and characterized them based on how they estimate probe-space uncertainty and propagate the correction through the representation. In addition, we propose Fit-Path, a solver designed to achieve strong global and local control. Our results in four control setups (class, attributes, foreground, and keypoints) show that LiSM methods, and Fit-Path in particular, provide effective, lightweight control across global and local tasks, outperforming noise-aware and pixel-space guidance.
comment: Project page: https://penway.cn/lism/
☆ SHARPnP: Self-Supervised and Plug-and-Play Hyperspectral Super-Resolution from Real Noisy Unaligned Camera Measurements
Mohamad Jouni, Brayan Monroy, Jorge Bacca, Mauro Dalla Mura
Affordable snapshot hyperspectral cameras capture spectral images in a single exposure but suffer from limited spatial resolution and sensor noise. Low-cost RGB cameras provide fine visible details to guide NIR reconstruction, but introduce spatially varying cross-camera misalignment. Supervised fusion methods require relatively large datasets of clean, high-resolution hyperspectral images, are sensitive to sensor noise, and generalize poorly across new sensors. We introduce SHARPnP, an interpretable, flexible framework coupling registration and reconstruction for RGB-guided hyperspectral super-resolution from noisy, unaligned measurements without clean references. We adapt a pretrained registration model via a cross-view loss backpropagated through a fixed plug-and-play fusion module. Temporal and recorrupted pairs enable reference-free self-supervision on noisy inputs. At test time, we calibrate cross-camera radiometry and refine alignment. Plug-and-play fusion employs sequential three-band denoising. On the REAL benchmark, SHARPnP outperforms supervised fusion baselines at $4\times$, $8\times$, and $16\times$ on clean inputs and at $4\times$ under Gaussian noise ($σ=5/255, 10/255$). On native RGB-HSI snapshot measurements, it reconstructs all 51 VIS-NIR bands, beyond the conventional 31-band VIS setting, without high-resolution references.
☆ GRAPE-Bench: When Vision Degrades, Does Video Reasoning Hold?
Ce Zhang, Junyi He, Tianshi Ming, Jinxi He, Jianshu Zhang, Xiyuan Yang, Jianuo Zhu, Yicheng Tao, Xiyu Luo, Minghao Fu, Jiahui Zhu, Kehan Guo, Yunzhong Xiao, Jingyang Lin, Wei Chow, Lingdong Kong, Katia Sycara, Yaqi Xie
Despite strong performance on standard benchmarks, video reasoning models remain vulnerable to visual degradation, raising concerns about their reliability in safety-critical scenarios. Existing benchmarks address this concern in part by simulating visual degradation or probing model reasoning with challenging questions, leaving open how well models handle naturally degraded video and whether they can make the simpler judgments that matter for safe driving. To this end, we introduce GRAPE-Bench, which jointly evaluates video reasoning across visual degradation conditions and question difficulty. It combines a synthetic set spanning twelve corruption types across daily-life and driving videos with real-world footage of driving at night or in rain, snow, or fog. Each video is paired with three progressively challenging questions, from fundamental judgments with potential safety implications to demanding reasoning stress tests. Across open-weight and frontier models, we observe ranking reversals between synthetic and real-world conditions and level-specific weaknesses obscured by overall accuracy. Synthetic-data fine-tuning improves Qwen3.5-9B's real-world accuracy from 76.7% to 81.1%, while clean-privileged on-policy distillation reaches 80.4% in a separate reasoning-enabled setting. Through preference steering, we further demonstrate continuous control over a frozen model's trade-off between safety-relevant judgments and challenging reasoning, with little change in overall accuracy. Together, GRAPE-Bench provides a unified testbed for evaluating, improving, and controlling video reasoning under degraded visual conditions.

☆ E-MAPS: Event-Based Promptable Video Segmentation with Memory-as-Prompt
Adonay Demewez Gebremedhin, Mohamad Alansari, Wessam Shehieb, Muzammal Naseer, Hasan AlMarzouqi, Sajid Javed, Naoufel Werghi
RGB-based video object segmentation (VOS) remains brittle under fast motion and adverse illumination. Event cameras preserve signal under blur and challenging exposure, but provide little evidence when motion slows. Interaction can restore object state for subsequent propagation, yet promptable event methods merely address single windows. We formalize event-based Promptable Video Segmentation (ePVS), where prompts at arbitrary windows initialize, correct, or introduce objects and predictions. We present Event Memory-As-Prompt Segmentation (E-MAPS), which transfers a pretrained promptable segmenter to event streams and learns propagation and correction. Event-to-Token (E2T) aligns recurrent event features with pretrained representations while preserving prompt-conditioning priors. Memory-Aware Prompting (MAP) converts object-conditioned history into sparse prompts, allowing memory and user inputs to share one decoder pathway efficiently. We construct Event-View Masklets (EViM) from 206K aligned RGB-event pairs and 620K masks for two-stage representation transfer and native event-video learning, and establish three training-disjoint benchmarks. E-MAPS leads prompt-once and interactive ePVS across all three benchmarks while being more efficient. It further demonstrates strong performance on zero-shot object tracking benchmarks. Project page: https://github.com/adonaydem/emaps-wacv
☆ RePix-VFI: Re-rendering Observed Pixels for Video Frame Interpolation with Generative Priors from One-Step Diffusion
Dayeon Kim, Jeonghyeok Do, Munchurl Kim
Multi-frame video frame interpolation (VFI) aims to reconstruct dense video from sparse keyframes, requiring accurate intermediate motion and faithful appearance. As temporal gaps grow, flow-based methods can retain observed textures but misplace them under ambiguous motion, whereas iterative latent-diffusion models can synthesize plausible content but incur substantial sampling costs and may alter details during reconstruction with a variational autoencoder (VAE). We present RePix-VFI, named for Re-rendering observed Pixels, a multi-frame VFI framework that couples draft-conditioned one-step video diffusion with reconstruction from observed keyframes. A pretrained video diffusion model refines a flow-rendered draft of the whole window in a single forward pass. For each target frame, our generative readback matches its two bounding keyframes to the generated prediction using an optical-flow estimator. The resulting correspondences guide re-rendering of original keyframe RGB pixels outside the VAE. A lightweight appearance fusion head combines these renderings with generated appearance. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate significant improvements in reconstruction and perceptual quality. On SNU-FILM at $\times$8 and $\times$16, RePix-VFI achieves the highest PSNR and the lowest LPIPS, FloLPIPS, and tOF among the compared methods, exceeding the best evaluated diffusion-based baseline by 1.71 and 1.48dB in PSNR, respectively. It also runs 32--42$\times$ faster than the state-of-the-art multi-frame VFI diffusion model.

☆ Training Lightweight Gaze Models without Target Gaze Annotation: What Makes a Good Teacher?
Scott J. Lewis, Di Fu
Model-generated labels offer a scalable route to training lightweight vision models, but what makes a model a good teacher, and can we tell before training a student? We study this in gaze target estimation, where interactive robots need models that are both accurate and efficient. In a controlled comparison of eleven supervision conditions, we vary only the source of gaze-point labels, keeping the student, training protocol and 361k training samples fixed, across three video datasets, two student sizes and three seeds; every student is evaluated against human annotation. Three findings emerge. First, imperfect model-generated labels can replace human annotation: Gaze-LLE, never trained on the target datasets' gaze annotation, trains students that match annotation-trained ones on ViT-Tiny and are significantly more accurate on ViT-Small (average distance error 0.187 vs 0.196), and the ViT-Tiny student runs 32$\times$ faster than its teacher on a laptop CPU. Second, apparent competence can conceal unreliable supervision: given another person's face centre in the prompt, InternVL3 and Qwen3-VL return it on 93.4% and 81.1% of test samples, and a copy-the-coordinate baseline matches InternVL3's labels and students. Without that coordinate, both models fall far behind the specialist. Third, good teachers can be identified before training: validation label error ranks student test error (Spearman's $ρ= 0.91$), and ten annotated clips single out the two specialist teachers in 95% of draws. These findings give practical principles for assessing supervision, exposing shortcuts and selecting teachers for lightweight models.

☆ RFW-W: Scaling Physical Asset Universes for Generative Embodied Simulation
Jiawei Weng, Rui Zhang, Saining Zhang, Changjian Pan, Yuanbo Lyu, Jiarui Guo, Yongzhi Li, Guolin Liu, Jialu Liu, Jiankun Wang, Yi Yang, Peishuo Li, Zhiheng Li, Jiaying Wan, Junhao Chen, Weiqing Xiao, Jingrun Du, Wenyi Li, Weiyi Lin, Zenan Meng, Hu Wei, Lin Qu, Zongzheng Zhang, Hao Zhao, Chaojian Li
Scaling embodied simulation requires diverse objects with executable physical representations. We present RFW-W, a physical asset universe connecting rigid, articulated, and deformable asset sources to task-conditioned scene composition. Its reported inventories comprise 1,010,386 asset records: 524,611 rigid assets in 1,212 categories (RFW-R), 402,410 articulated assets in 531 categories (RFW-A), and 83,365 jointly verified deformables in 485 categories (RFW-S). These taxonomies contribute 2,228 dataset--category entries. RFW-R couples category-guided generation with collision geometry, composed physical properties, and interaction annotations; RFW-A uses reusable agent-authored procedural generators with explicit part and joint structure; RFW-S uses structure-aware simulation representations, calibration, and independent testing. A common interface preserves physical requirements specific to each asset type for retrieval and scene assembly. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate that RFW-R provides broader asset coverage and stronger scene-fulfillment capabilities than existing datasets. Across five RoboTwin tasks, using 100 demonstrations per task for each asset source, policies trained on RFW-R achieve macro success rates of 71.2% in clean settings and 41.8% under randomization, exceeding the strongest baseline by 15.8 and 10.6 percentage points, respectively. RFW-W provides a scalable and unified asset foundation for generating physically grounded, task-conditioned embodied worlds.
