☆ Counterfactual Velocity Steering for World Action Models
Xufeng Zhan, Yuanzhi Liang, Ye Lu, Haibin Huang, Chi Zhang, Xuelong Li
Flow-based robot policies generate actions by repeatedly evaluating a conditional velocity field, so test-time bias correction seems simple: query the action expert under a task-agnostic condition and subtract that velocity from the task-conditioned prediction. We show this is often wrong. On Fast-WAM across 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, mean-instruction predictions align strongly with task-conditioned velocities (cosine approximately 0.94-0.95). Averaging eight completed-state references barely cancels this direction: their mean norm is 98.3% of the mean individual norm. References thus contain a large shared transport component, not only harmful bias, and aggressive subtraction damages generation. We propose a same-state diagnostic and shrinkage analysis showing that the optimal correction scale depends on reference signal-to-noise. This motivates geometry-calibrated action debiasing, which removes only the component orthogonal to the task velocity and predicts a small task-dependent scale from instruction geometry. In controlled RoboTwin experiments, corrupting instructions still permits 25.1% success (50 tasks, 20 episodes), whereas dynamic visual corruption nearly eliminates success. A fixed centered orthogonal correction reaches 92.7% versus a 92.1% baseline in one randomized 1000-trial sweep, but gains are non-monotonic and within run-to-run variation. An angular scale pilot has an offline oracle-gated bound of 94.5%; its best learned online realization reaches 92.5%. These results identify shared flow and train-serve mismatch as central obstacles and provide a reproducible foundation for conditional correction.
☆ Calibrating World Action Models: From Adaptive System 2 Takeover to Self-Evolution
Wenhao Li, Yu Han, Xiu Su, Dehao Wu, Keke Huang, Shan You, Fei Wang, Chang Xu
World action models (WAMs) deliver fast visuomotor control, yet degrade sharply in challenging scenes and act blindly when about to fail; conversely, foundation-model-based agents generalize and recover reliably, but incur prohibitive latency and cost when queried at every step. To achieve both WAM (System 1)-level speed and agent (System 2)-level reliability--- we propose \textbf{\oursfull (\ours)}, a framework that calibrates WAMs' confidence--- adaptively triggering System~2 only when necessary, and distilling System~2's knowledge to form an evolving System~1. First, \ours equips a frozen WAM with \textbf{calibrated self-assessment}: a single lightweight judgment token reading internal video--action features is trained via our proposed \textbf{cross-fitted temporal-difference (TD) learning} using only binary rollout success/failure signals. It can predict a \textbf{calibrated success probability} at negligible overhead without affecting action predictions. Second, this calibrated success probability schedules control chunk by chunk---invoking System~2 to resolve bottlenecks when confidence drops, and handing control back to the WAM once confidence recovers, preserving WAM-like speed while approaching System~2 reliability. Third, as System~2 intervenes only when the WAM lacks confidence, its takeover trajectories directly capture the WAM's capability gaps. JiL distills these takeovers into the WAM to repair those gaps so System~1 can operate standalone without System~2 at test time, while our mastered-skill anchoring and dynamic confidence gating prevent degrading existing capabilities.
☆ OmniSLAM: Evidence-Authorized Revision of Persistent Object Maps
Haoxiang Jie, Yaoyuan Yan, Zhiyou Heng, Liang Li, Zhaosong Li, Lifeng Liu
Persistent object maps must incorporate new surfaces while retaining valid identities and correcting earlier associations. We present a map-revision module that separates historical identity changes from new-surface admission. Proposed merges are tested against shared and separate mask explanations across views; a merge is allowed only if its evidence margin remains positive after removing any one observed frame. New measured points are assigned through local identity competition, with a mask witness and a seed-frame stability check. On two preselected KITTI-360 windows, the fixed method increases mean building/car instance AP50:90 from 17.259 to 18.762 under a local evaluation protocol. Controlled output interventions attribute the gains to fragment consolidation, protection against harmful overwrites, and local assignment of new points. Four additional spatial holdouts increase mean AP from 20.263 to 23.171, although unconditional revision is slightly higher at 23.251. The extra seed-frame check yields no AP gain over nearest-seed assignment in either set. A 330-frame garage recording demonstrates offline integration with LiDAR--inertial--visual odometry. These results identify where observation-supported revision improves object maps and where conservative decisions still limit recovery.
☆ Trustworthy agentic lunar robotics: safety-constrained contingent planning with a foundation-model planner
Bingqi Huang, Bingchuan Wei, Yingkai Cai, Zhaokui Wang
Sustained lunar-base operations require robots that restore equipment and deliver cargo under conditions unforeseen before deployment. Flown space autonomy executes pre-validated procedures and enters a safe hold outside their scope, whereas foundation models synthesize plans on site that cannot be verified before execution. We formulate these operations as safety-constrained contingent planning with irreversible actions, erroneous records, three-valued physical evidence, and costly, deadline-constrained sensing. We propose asymmetric knowledge-level replanning (AKR), which treats the planner as an untrusted black box: reversible actions run on the planner's assumptions, and irreversible actions run only after a minimum-cost sensing cover verifies every precondition. Under sound measurements, no irreversible action executes on a false precondition for any planner or record, the sensing cost before an irreversible action is bounded below for every sound knowledge-based policy, and execution with a complete planner ends in a verified goal or a certified hold. AKR executed no hazardous action in 21,000 Monte Carlo trials with sound observations or in 58 full-stack runs; the FF-Replan acting rule executed one in 7% of those trials. The median AKR run took 1.10 times the fastest run on the same mission, against 1.50 under the K-replanner acting rule. AKR completed 20 of 21 contingency and sequential-fault runs with an unchanged task model; the original PLEXIL and EUROPA$\rightarrow$PLEXIL procedures completed none.
☆ Quantizing in the Loop: Drift-Aware Ultra-Low-Bit Vision-Language-Action Models
Yanlong Chen, Thongthornpatch Chamadol, Yichen Guo, Yunfei Gao, Mohan Liu, Addison Lin Wang, Yawei Li
Deploying large vision-language-action (VLA) models on resource-constrained robots demands extreme compression, yet existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods frequently collapse at ultra-low bit-widths ($\le$ 2 bits). We trace this failure to two mismatches in standard pipelines. First, calibrating on static offline demonstrations induces distribution shift: minor quantization perturbations drive the policy into unseen states where uncalibrated errors compound. Second, minimizing the layer-wise weight reconstruction error is a flawed proxy, as action generation depends only on the representations consumed by the action head. We present LoopQ, an on-policy ultra-low-bit quantization framework. LoopQ closes the loop by calibrating on states from the quantized policy's own rollouts. It then adds readout-aligned fine-tuning, which freezes the trellis codes and optimizes only lightweight lookup tables and scaling factors to align the backbone readout with the full-precision teacher. With all linear layers at 2 bits, LoopQ achieves a 60.4% success rate on LIBERO-Plus with GR00T N1.7, close to the 61.8% of full precision. Even at 1 bit per weight, $π_{0.5}$ still completes 80.0% of LIBERO tasks. With 8-bit activations, the 2-bit $π_{0.5}$ runs on integer kernels on an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor, with 4.1$\times$ smaller weights and 44% less memory. On a real AgileX Piper arm, it stays within one success of full precision on each of three tasks. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/LoopQ

☆ Confidently Lost: Silent Failure and Edge Deployment of Dense Visual SLAM under Photon Starvation ICRA 2027
Shrikrishna Bhagirath Rajule, Srinath Neelamagam, Aniket Bera
Dense visual SLAM built on learned two-view geometry is evaluated in good light; in low light it fails silently. Two frames of 9-level quantized noise, no scene at all, give MASt3R-SLAM's network a cross-view geometric self-consistency of 0.936; a real dark frame pair gives 0.935. Starved of structure, the network invents the same geometry for both views and the system trusts the agreement: on a dark sequence it consumes 1,605 frames, emits 7 keyframes, rejects no factor-graph edges and reports full frame rate, while over 95% of the correspondences it accepts violate the ground-truth epipolar geometry. One inflated statistic is read by two subsystems against thresholds in opposite directions, so keyframing starves while relocalization accepts almost every candidate. The same statistic, read at keyframe-pair baselines, separates the confident collapse from working runs on the ETH3D dark sequences without ground truth or extra computation (in-sample). Low-light-adapted weights take tracked trajectories from 1/6 to 5/6, as does retuning two thresholds; neither yields accurate ones, because the adaptation withdraws confidence from wrong geometry rather than finding right geometry. Replayed on a Jetson AGX Orin carried by a legged robot, the mechanism's signature reproduces on the two darkest of four routes, and which of its faces appears varies with route geometry and sensor encoding. The network does not lose confidence in the dark; it manufactures it.

☆ LeadVLA: Learning Follower-Aware Route Execution for Robot Leading
Tianle Zeng, Hanjing Ye, Bingyi Xia, Yuchen Zhou, Zibo Zhang, Yufei Huang, Yonggen Ling, Hong Zhang
Robot leading requires executing a route while continuously adapting to a designated follower. Existing robot-leading systems often mediate follower understanding and physical route execution through explicit states, planners, or modular interfaces; directly learning this coupling through end-to-end trajectory prediction can instead entangle route execution with follower response. We introduce LeadVLA, a structured multimodal policy that preserves the route as an explicit Path reference while learning a Pace for route progress and a Residual for local follower- and scene-conditioned adaptation. To make this problem trainable and measurable, we develop LeadInfra, a configurable Unreal Engine-based closed-loop data-generation infrastructure from which we instantiate an approximately 4M-sample training corpus, and LeadBench, a standardized benchmark with 108 fully held-out closed-loop episodes. LeadVLA achieves the highest task success (39.6%) among evaluated robot policies on LeadBench while maintaining strong route fidelity and follower responsiveness, and transfers to unseen real-world environments without real-world policy fine-tuning. ☆ RMR-VLA: Recurrent Memory Reasoning for Vision-Language-Action Models
Yiheng Du, Jingqi Tian, Xu Jiang, Jiexuan Zhang, Shuyu Wang, Zecheng Tang, Jian Zhang
Long-horizon, history-dependent robotic manipulation often requires acting on visual cues that have disappeared, such as an object indicated earlier or a target hidden under a moving cup. The key challenge is to maintain what past evidence means for the next action as the scene changes. We introduce Recurrent Memory Reasoning (RMR), an explicit reasoning step that connects memory to action inside a vision-language-action model (VLA), with no external reasoning model. At each update, the VLA first infers an event from visual evidence, then revises the task state and grounds a subgoal in the current scene to guide action generation. Carrying the state and subgoal across updates lets remembered identities and task progress determine the current target, doubling RoboMME success over an otherwise identical model without recurrence. Joint training lets one VLA both reason and act; because its memory decisions are text tokens with exact likelihoods, GRPO refines them from rollout rewards without making action generation stochastic. Among the compared methods, RMR-VLA achieves the best results on RoboMME (66.46% overall, 79.83% on the Reference category) and LIBERO-Mem (90.08%).
☆ Value function based Reward shaping for safety in quadrupeds
Janani S K, Manan Tayal, Shishir N. Y Kolathaya
Reinforcement Learning (RL) has progressed from simple control tasks to complex real-world challenges with large state spaces. While RL excels in these tasks, training time remains a limitation. Reward shaping is a popular solution, but existing methods often rely on value functions, which face scalability issues. This paper presents a novel safety-oriented reward-shaping framework inspired by barrier functions, offering simplicity and ease of implementation across various environments and tasks. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed reward formulations, we conduct simulation experiments on the Unitree Go1 quadruped robot in Isaacgym. The policy was better than the existing baselines and reduced safety violations from 27% to 0.1% without almost any compromise on the performance.

♻ ☆ Learning from Failure: Robot Self-Improvement via Human Videos
Hanzhi Chen, Anran Zhang, Simon Schaefer, Kejia Chen, Shi Chen, Daniel Cremers, Oier Mees, Stefan Leutenegger
Learning from deployment experience is essential for robots to improve their performance in the real world. A robot should be able to learn from failed executions, but these do not reveal which actions would have succeeded, and obtaining corrections from human experts requires costly monitoring and intervention. Human videos offer a rich source of interaction experience, showing how actions change the environment and lead to task completion. To turn this experience into corrective supervision, we introduce Dynamics-Guided Action Correction (DGAC), which uses dynamics and value models pretrained on human videos to construct alternative actions at failed states and evaluate their outcomes without executing each candidate. We evaluate our method on seven real-world manipulation tasks across two robot embodiments and demonstrate that it improves the average success rate from 40% to 81%, requiring no expert corrections during self-improvement. We further show that generated corrections enable recovery from failed executions and provide more effective training targets than imagined policy rollouts using the same models and data. Finally, we demonstrate that human-video dynamics and value models provide effective corrective supervision for policies pretrained on either human or robot data, suggesting that human videos benefit robot learning in addition to policy initialization.

♻ ☆ Not All Features Are Created Equal: A Mechanistic Study of Vision-Language-Action Models NeurIPS 2026
Bryce Grant, Xijia Zhao, Peng Wang
A fine-tuned Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy can easily place the alphabet soup in the basket on command, just as it saw during fine-tuning. However, if the basket is shifted five centimeters to the left, it drops the soup off the table. We developed an interpretability pipeline to investigate what such a policy is computing. Injecting task A's activations into the action expert while the policy looks at task B's scene makes $π_{0.5}$ execute task A's motor trajectory in 99.6\% of episodes ($n{=}1{,}968$). The injected program is bound to absolute workspace coordinates and ignores the visible scene, which provides a mechanistic account of the perturbation brittleness that concurrent benchmarks report. The binding holds on a physical UR10e: directed replay redirects the commanded task in 26/26 rollouts in one direction and 18/26 in the other, with no-injection and random-direction controls at the floor, and once the source object is moved 10-15 cm the arm grasps and releases at the recorded coordinates in 50/50 trials, picking up the wrong block when one sits there and closing on empty air when none does. Applying the same interventions to five VLAs on LIBERO, MetaWorld, SimplerEnv, and ALOHA over $420{,}000+$ rollouts yields three further findings: every architecture encodes the instruction, and four of the five weight it below vision whenever the scene alone identifies the goal; under the standard replacement write-back the SAE pooling that preserves behavior is architecture-specific ($π_{0.5}$ per-token, SmolVLA indifferent), and goal selection and motor generation separate into VLM and expert pathways wherever the two are distinguishable. We release \textbf{Action Atlas} (https://action-atlas.com), an interactive platform covering all 520+ trained SAEs, 79 identified concepts, and the scored UR10e rollouts. Code: https://cwru-aism.github.io/vla-interp-page/
comment: NeurIPS 2026 Poster, ICLR Multimodal Intelligence Workshop Oral, 44 pages, 14 figures
♻ ☆ Making Koopman Control Guarantees Hold on Robots
Abulikemu Abuduweili, Changliu Liu
Koopman operator theory lets linear controllers handle nonlinear robots: an encoder lifts the state into a latent space with approximately linear dynamics, on which LQR or MPC is designed. A controller that stabilizes the latent model, however, may fail to stabilize the real nonlinear system. Stability is analyzed on latent rollouts, where the linear model propagates its own predictions, but on the robot the nonlinear dynamics produce each next state, which the controller re-encodes at every step. We prove that latent stability transfers to the robot when the latent model reproduces the true closed-loop dynamics to first order on the embedding's tangent space at the target. We also derive a margin for approximate matching and show that an open-loop stable latent model cannot match the plant's linearization at an unstable equilibrium. We propose Tangent-Invariant Koopman (TIK), which estimates a local plant linearization from offline transitions and builds first-order matching to it into the Koopman matrices. At the target, TIK's feedback gain equals the LQR gain of this linearization, and a bilinear input term models state-dependent actuation during large maneuvers. On four simulated open-loop unstable benchmarks, all 40 Standard Koopman controllers stabilize their latent models but are locally unstable on the real system, whereas all 40 TIK controllers stabilize it. An offline stability test with empirical curvature estimates identifies the stable TIK controllers on two cart-pole systems but is inconclusive under high noise. Given explicit model-error and curvature bounds, an invariant terminal set guarantees constraint satisfaction under local feedback after entry. TIK reaches 88% success in constrained cart-pole swing-up with a 0.25 ms planning budget and controls simulated seven-joint arms within 1~5 ms per step.
comment: https://walleclipse.github.io/tik-koopman/
♻ ☆ Sequential Planning via Anchored Robotic Keypoints
Bryce Grant, Aryeh Rothenberg, Logan Senning, Zonghe Chua, Zach Patterson, Peng Wang
Changes to what a robot can see do not mean that there is a change in the problem it is trying to solve, and many language-conditioned manipulation systems struggle with this distinction. When something in a scene moves, the robot might need to execute its actions in different places, but its manipulation plan can stay the same. We propose Sequential Planning via Anchored Robotic Keypoints (SPARK), which describes a task as a symbolic behavior tree that we anchor to the current 3D observations when each action is called. By verifying the plan at runtime we can recover from failures locally and anchor the objects to the scene again. We ask for a new plan only if this fails. We isolate this concept by taking a fixed plan and moving objects in the scene while executing. When displacing objects by $10$\,cm mid-episode we were still able to complete $60.0\%$ of trials with scene-diff verification and layered recovery, and we did not have to change the plan. Without practicing on the tasks being tested or using ground-truth object poses from the simulator during rollouts, we test our system (with one open-weight 27B planner with 4-bit weights) on LIBERO-PRO. Under this protocol, SPARK achieves a mean success of $74.4\%$ across the 6 position and task settings when the robot decides to retry from its own checks, and $77.8\%$ when it also reads a success check after each attempt. We also achieve a $75\%$ success rate across 11 physical task-embodiment settings on 3 different robots. Our work demonstrates that for an important class of failures, the robot does not need to ask for a new plan for its task. It can be enough to update the system's view of the world. Code is at https://github.com/CWRU-AISM/sparkbot and videos are at https://cwru-aism.github.io/spark-page/

♻ ☆ Perception-Aware Multi-UAV Implicit Coordination in the Wild
Manuel Boldrer, Michal Kamler, Afzal Ahmad, Martin Saska
We present a perception-aware 3D navigation system for decentralized multi-robot coordination in cluttered environments, such as forests with dense canopy cover where GNSS is unavailable. Our novel perception-aware approach computes collision-free motion toward a goal region while accounting for the limited field of view of the sensor, and is combined with a replanner to guide multiple robots to their goal. The system relies on an onboard anisotropic 3D LiDAR, used for localization, mapping, and detection of obstacles and neighboring robots. Decentralized coordination among the robots emerges as a byproduct of local interactions and common rules, so no explicit communication is required. The system is evaluated through extensive single and multi-robot simulations across diverse scenarios and validated in multiple real-world field experiments.
♻ ☆ PAC-ACT: Post-training Actor-Critic for Action Chunking Transformers
Yujie Pang, Zudong Li, Leran Chen, Yongsheng Ma
Precision industrial contact manipulation requires reliable robot policies under pose perturbations and contact-force constraints. Vision-language-action models offer broad generalization but often introduce high inference latency and GPU-memory cost, while vision-action chunking policies are more suitable for real-time industrial control. However, these policies are usually trained by behavior cloning and suffer from distribution shift in contact-rich tasks. This paper proposes PAC-ACT, a reinforcement-learning post-training framework for pretrained Action Chunking Transformer policies. PAC-ACT reformulates policy optimization at the chunk level, constructs an ACT-transferred actor-critic architecture, and introduces a hybrid behavior-prior constraint to preserve the pretrained action distribution during online fine-tuning. Experiments on industrial precision-contact benchmarks show that PAC-ACT improves task success, contact stability, and force safety while retaining low latency and low GPU-memory usage. On the Contour task, PAC-ACT significantly reduces peak contact force and decreases the proportion of force readings above 60 N by 46 times. Sparse-reward ablations further show that the proposed behavior-prior constraint enables effective exploration under randomized initial poses.
comment: Revised version with clarified methodology, updated experimental analysis, and improved presentation
♻ ☆ Autonomous Mobile Robots on a Computing Field
Yonghwan Kim, Gil-Tak Kong, Un-Sook Choi
We introduce CABOT, a computational model for autonomous mobile robots in which the discrete plane the robots operate on is not a passive stage but an active computing medium. In the classical Look-Compute-Move (LCM) model every increase in computational capability is obtained by strengthening the robots themselves, with lights, memory or wider visibility, at a cost paid once per robot. CABOT strengthens the environment instead: each cell of the grid holds a state from a finite set Q, the states evolve synchronously under a uniform local rule that also senses whether a robot stands on the cell, that is, the floor is a cellular automaton, and the Look operation returns the states of the visible cells in addition to the positions of the visible robots. The robots are as weak as we can make them: oblivious, silent, lightless, myopic with visibility range 1, without multiplicity detection and unable to write to the floor. The number of field states |Q|, rather than any robot capability, becomes the measure of the resources required. On an inert floor (|Q| = 1) such robots can neither form a line, nor gather from scattered positions, nor explore a grid. We show that a handful of states changes this. Line Formation from connected configurations is solvable with four states, and field-silently, so that the floor also reaches a fixed point, with five. Gathering from arbitrary, possibly disconnected, configurations is solvable with three states and Line Formation from arbitrary configurations with six; we prove that neither can be solved field-silently with any number of states. A single robot explores every finite grid forever with four states and every torus with two, which is optimal. Further rule sets, validated by simulation only, equalize the spacing of robots on a row, fill a pattern painted on the floor and guide robots through a maze, and indicate the range of the model.

♻ ☆ NEXUS: Perceptive Whole-Body Control for Terrain-Adaptive Teleoperation
Xiangyu Miao, Junsong Wu, Jiyuan Shi, Weiji Xie, Jinrui Han, Xingyi Wang, Weinan Zhang, Chenjia Bai, Xuelong Li
Whole-body teleoperation requires a humanoid robot to reproduce a human operator's behavior even when their terrains differ. This demands that the robot perceive local terrain and adapt its posture and contacts accordingly, rather than copy the operator's motion frame by frame. However, paired motion data linking the same behaviors across flat ground and different terrains remain scarce, limiting supervision for learning terrain-adaptive control. To enable whole-body teleoperation across mismatched terrains, we introduce NEXUS, a perceptive whole-body control framework that combines human motion commands with onboard sensory feedback. We first develop a scalable terrain-aware adaptation algorithm that efficiently generates high-quality motion pairs across motions and terrains without per-motion or per-terrain tuning. Using a paired motion corpus totaling nearly 1,000 hours, we train a perceptive whole-body controller through teacher-student learning to reproduce commanded behaviors across terrains. Experiments demonstrate efficient, scalable generation of high-quality motion data and show that NEXUS combines broad behavioral coverage with terrain adaptability and tracking fidelity, outperforming existing whole-body controllers on the evaluated benchmarks. Zero-shot real-world deployment enables real-time whole-body teleoperation on diverse unseen terrains, further validating the generalization of our method. Project website: https://nexus-humanoid.github.io/
♻ ☆ RAGrasp: Geometry-Semantic Template Retrieval and Grasp Transfer
Shenzhe Zhu, Chengxiao He, Jan Harder
We present RAGrasp, a retrieval-augmented pipeline for planar parallel-jaw grasping from a compact set of locally collected, grasp-annotated RGB-D (color and depth) templates. Unlike task-specific predictors trained primarily on large public or synthetic grasp datasets, RAGrasp requires no end-to-end retraining for a new deployment.Its template memory is constructed from observations collected with the deployment camera, robot, and gripper in the target workspace, thereby aligning stored examples with the local sensing and embodiment conditions. The system uses self-supervised DINOv2 visual fea- tures together with appearance and depth cues to prompt the Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2), which isolates the query object. A two-stage geometry-semantic retrieval cascade then selects a template, and a confidence gate chooses one of two grasp- transfer estimators. The transferred grasp is refined using mask- support and silhouette-contact constraints before calibrated 2D- to-3D conversion. In real-world trials, RAGrasp achieves 20/20 successful grasps on seen objects and 19/20 on unseen objects. Within the evaluated setting, the results demonstrate deployment- specific grasp adaptation from limited local annotation and tolerance to the tested viewpoint and illumination changes.
♻ ☆ A Bi-level Co-design Framework for Lunar Monoped with 2D Jump and Landing Control
Sanjay Ramkumar, Suraj Kumar
Legged robots for lunar exploration must be designed for low gravity, where reduced contact forces and long flight phases make leg morphology and controller choice interdependent. We study this for a planar monoped in lunar gravity (1.625 m/s^2) using a bi-level co-design framework: a differential evolution outer loop searches over link lengths, and each candidate is evaluated on a vertical jump by either a quadratic program based task-space controller (QP-TSC) or a direct-collocation based trajectory optimization. The two controllers yield different optimal link lengths, and trajectory optimization outperforms the QP-TSC across most of the design space, with 17% lower Cost of Transport (COT) at their respective optima. We then extend to a 2D jump, where trajectory optimization with centroidal angular momentum regulation produces stable in-place and forward jumps, and an LQR controller absorbs impact and stabilizes the robot after touchdown. This is demonstrated on a baseline morphology with both links 0.3 m long.

♻ ☆ LiteNWM: Efficient Latent World Models for Onboard Visual Navigation in the Wild
Linkai Liu, Yuntian Zhang, Zhenshan Bing, Chen Chen, Lingjuan Lyu, Shangguang Wang, Mengwei Xu, Dongqi Cai
Direct visual navigation policies generate trajectories efficiently but do not explicitly evaluate their future consequences. Generative navigation world models provide this foresight through visual rollouts, which are costly when evaluating multiple candidates. We present LiteNWM, a latent navigation world model that shares visual encoding across candidates and jointly predicts their action-conditioned future representations at multiple horizons, while a learned scorer uses these predictions to select trajectories. In offline evaluations on RECON, SCAND, and SACSoN, LiteNWM reduces macro-averaged trajectory error by 17.56% relative to NoMaD+NWM-XL and achieves a 128.00-fold end-to-end speedup on an RTX 5090. The same evaluator transfers from NoMaD to MBRA without proposer-specific retraining, reducing MBRA's macro-averaged trajectory error by 16.2%. In real-robot experiments in unseen indoor and outdoor environments, LiteNWM improves navigation success from 43.3% to 83.3% relative to NoMaD. These results demonstrate that LiteNWM can be deployed for future-aware planning and closed-loop navigation on a physical robot.

♻ ☆ OASIS: From Simulation Data Collection to Real-World Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
Zehao Yu, Jiakun Zheng, Weiji Xie, Jiyuan Shi, Chenyun Zhang, Chenjia Bai, Xuelong Li
Recent progress in robot manipulation has been largely driven by learning from large-scale demonstrations. For humanoid robot loco-manipulation tasks, however, existing data sources force an unsatisfying tradeoff between trajectory quality and scalability. Real-world teleoperation provides the highest-quality trajectories but requires dedicated physical space and time-consuming scene resets. Simulation offers an alternative way out of this dilemma: it can produce clean, embodiment-aligned data at scale without any physical hardware. In this paper, we propose OASIS, a simulation-data-driven framework for humanoid loco-manipulation. OASIS automatically reconstructs realistic object assets from real-world images using a 3D generative model. Based on these assets, trajectories are first collected through teleoperation in simulation, and then augmented under diverse domain randomizations in a post-processing stage. With the resulting simulation data, we further design a hierarchical visuomotor policy for humanoid loco-manipulation. Extensive experiments on the real humanoid robot show that, under zero-shot deployment, the policy trained on our simulation data achieves higher success rates on most tasks than that trained on real-robot teleoperation data, owing largely to the broad lighting and environmental variations covered by our simulation rendering, which real-robot data fails to capture. The project page is available at https://oasis-humanoid.github.io/.

♻ ☆ Video2Track: Steerable Adversarial Scenario Generation from Real-World Interaction Videos to Proving Grounds for Automated Driving System Testing
Mengjie Tian, Xinrui Zhang, Tianyu Li, Peizhi Zhang, Guirong Zhuo, Haojie Feng, Ziyi Yin, Qixiang Zhang, Lu Xiong
Physical proving-ground testing enables controlled and repeatable validation of automated driving systems (ADSs). However, existing approaches often rely on manually designed reference routes and scripted vehicle behaviors, limiting deployment efficiency, real-world interaction reproduction, and interaction risk steerability. To address these limitations, we propose Video2Track, a framework that converts real-world driving videos into steerable adversarial scenarios for proving-ground testing. Video2Track extracts interaction semantics using a vision-language model, retrieves compatible maneuver pairs on the target road network, and generates reference trajectories through interaction-guided diffusion. Game-based online refinement adjusts background vehicle (BV) trajectories based on real-time feedback from the vehicle under test (VUT) to regulate interaction risk toward a prescribed anticipated post-encroachment time (APET). Video2Track achieved an interaction consistency rate of 82.1\% and a scenario generation success rate of 78.6\%. In proving-ground tests, the mean minimum APET was within 0.5~s of each of the four target values. Video2Track also achieved lower mean minimum APET values than the evaluated baselines in both cut-in and unprotected left-turn scenarios. These results demonstrate the feasibility of transferring real-world driving interactions to executable proving-ground scenarios, enabling faithful interaction reproduction and steerable adversarial testing on an Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled 5G cloud-controlled platform.

♻ ☆ Self-Supervised Online Robot-Agnostic Traversability Estimation for Open-World Environments
Julia Hindel, Simon Bultmann, Houman Masnavi, Daniele Cattaneo, Abhinav Valada
Self-supervised online traversability estimation enables robots to continuously learn from unlabeled open-world experiences and adapt their navigation behavior toward safe and efficient trajectories. Existing approaches either rely on handcrafted proprioceptive traversability scores, limiting robot-agnosticism, or cluster prior data, preventing online learning. Moreover, many continual learning methods incur substantial memory and computational costs, hindering onboard deployment. We introduce COTRATE, an online learning framework for continuous traversability estimation from multimodal, unlabeled robot experience. Our method first infers robust traversability scores using a robot-agnostic, learning-based online terrain assessment module operating on proprioceptiveand inertial signals. These scores then supervise a visual traversability network through a novel alignment loss that associates visual embeddings with online terrain assessments. To mitigate forgetting during continual learning with minimal overhead, we propose a diversity-aware feature selection strategythat preserves performance using a compact replay memory. We further show that the learned traversability representation supports knowledge transfer across different robot platforms with different locomotion kinematics. We evaluate COTRATE on a dataset of $\approx$ 50,000 images collected with two robotic platforms across 11 outdoor terrains, and benchmark it on navigation tasks in three representative outdoor environments. We make the dataset, code, and trained models publicly available.

♻ ☆ PhysMoE: Fast Spatial Grounding with Single-Token Coordinate Representation in Modality-Decoupled VLMs
Ruimeng Liu, Denan Liang, Kuan Xu, Ruofei Bai, Fuming Zhang, Shenghai Yuan, Lihua Xie
Embodied Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are backbones for robotic planning and manipulation. However, for coordinate prediction in grounding tasks, existing architectures suffer from two distinct bottlenecks: discrete tokenization disrupts spatial continuity with high decoding latency, while standard point regression fails on multi-contact affordances and irregularly shaped targets. To resolve these challenges, we propose PhysMoE, introducing three core contributions: (1) sharing lower layers for multimodal context while routing upper layers to specialized spatial (pixel) and linguistic (text) experts by physical modality, eliminating gradient interference; (2) encoding each coordinate as a single token by reusing the visual encoder's learned positional embeddings, injecting 2D spatial priors to natively align coordinates with visual features and ease training; and (3) differentiable Signed Distance Field (SDF) supervision on pointing, accommodating affordances and irregular geometries without costly mask decoders. Compared to base models, PhysMoE achieves a 15.7% average gain and an 8.31x throughput speedup across 9 coordinate-based grounding benchmarks (trajectory, affordance, and localization), while preserving multimodal understanding and reasoning across 11 text-based embodied benchmarks. Our work is open-sourced at https://github.com/lrm20011/ps_moe_open.
♻ ☆ YUBI: Yielding Universal Bidigital Interface for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation at Scale
Takehiko Ohkawa, Jumpei Arima, Yuki Noguchi, Masatoshi Tateno, Makoto Sugiura, Takuya Okubo, Kengo Ikeuchi, Yuma Shin, Hiroki Nishizawa, Naoaki Kanazawa, Yuki Wakayama, Daiki Fukunaga, Koshi Makihara, Tomohiro Motoda, Floris Erich, Yukiyasu Domae, Tatsuya Matsushima, Yohishiro Okumatsu, Kei Ota
We introduce Yielding Universal Bidigital Interface (YUBI), a finger-aligned gripper designed to enable intuitive, ergonomic, and scalable data collection for bimanual dexterous manipulation. While handheld data collection systems such as Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) enable affordable data collection, their bulky pistol-grip designs can pose ergonomic and usability challenges for fine-grained, dexterous manipulation tasks. To address this, YUBI presents a distinct design principle: yielding, finger-driven actuation that directly maps human finger movements to gripper jaw motion. Using the YUBI devices, we set up a data collection system with integrated VR-based 6 DoF tracking of the gripper, ensuring high-fidelity trajectory data acquisition. We curate a UMI-based dataset of unprecedented scale: 8,434 hours across 1.20M episodes and 119 tasks. Experiments show that YUBI offers advantages over the UMI gripper in versatility for complex bimanual tasks, dexterity, and operational efficiency. A single policy trained on the YUBI dataset transfers across multiple bimanual robots (UR, Franka, and ELEY) simply by mounting the gripper on each platform, confirming that the collected data are directly executable as policy supervision. We release the gripper hardware, data-collection software, and dataset as one integrated stack, offering the open community a reproducible path to large-scale data acquisition for advancing robotic foundation models.

♻ ☆ DynEoMT: Learning Object Dynamicity from Online Segmentation Queries
Calvin Galagain, Martyna Poreba, François Goulette
Video segmentation models delineate and associate regions over time, but do not explicitly indicate whether they move independently of the camera. Query-based architectures propagate region representations across frames, raising a central question: can existing segmentation queries also support dynamicity prediction? We introduce DynEoMT, which adds a lightweight dynamicity head to existing segmentation queries without altering the segmentation or query-propagation architecture. To supervise this additional task, we generate class-agnostic pseudo-labels offline from camera-compensated optical flow. At inference, DynEoMT requires only the current frame and propagated queries, without explicit motion or geometric inputs. On VIPSeg, an MLP probe trained on frozen ViT-L queries achieves conditional balanced accuracy within 0.05 percentage points of full fine-tuning, suggesting that dynamicity-relevant information is already accessible in these representations. Across VIPSeg, OVIS, YouTube-VIS 2022, and VSPW, the ViT-B variant achieves conditional balanced accuracies of 84.30%, 67.98%, 68.59%, and 87.64%, respectively, while largely preserving segmentation performance with minimal overhead in the measured inference path.
♻ ☆ Safe Task Completion via Graph-Based Planning for LLM-Powered Robots
Ali Taheri, Alireza Taban, Qizhou Wang, Wanhua Li
Large Language Models (LLMs) are used to drive robotic manipulation and planning, yet deploying them on physical systems exposes risks, including jailbreak attacks that induce unsafe behavior. Existing inference-time defenses are mostly evaluated on short instructions with a single hazard. Real tasks may mix safe and unsafe sub-tasks, or combine individually safe actions into an unsafe outcome. For such compound instructions, a single safety decision either misses the hazard or rejects the whole instruction. We introduce safe task completion, a task that requires an LLM-powered robot to refuse the harmful part of an instruction while completing its legitimate part. To address this, we propose RuleGraph, a multi-agent Graph-of-Rules framework that verifies safety at multiple stages rather than relying on a single one. Five agents ground safety principles into world-specific rules, judge each sub-task in context, and derive a safe goal from the legitimate ones. Planning toward this goal is organized as a graph in which each node handles its assigned rules. Candidate plans are verified and aggregated level by level until one plan satisfies every rule. We evaluate RuleGraph on pure-attack and compound instructions from two benchmarks, measuring Attack Success Rate (ASR) and Task Success Rate (TSR). RuleGraph reaches 0% ASR on both benchmarks and highest TSR among all methods, with 98.57% on the RoboGuard benchmark and 83.51% on our long-horizon compound instructions.
♻ ☆ To New Beginnings: A Survey of Unified Perception in Autonomous Vehicle Software
Loic Stratil, Felix Fent, Esteban Rivera, Markus Lienkamp
Autonomous vehicle perception typically relies on modular pipelines that decompose the task into detection, tracking, and prediction. While interpretable, these pipelines suffer from error accumulation and limited inter-task synergy. Unified perception has emerged as a promising paradigm that integrates these sub-tasks within a shared architecture, potentially improving robustness, contextual reasoning, and efficiency while retaining interpretable outputs. In this survey, we provide a comprehensive overview of unified perception, introducing a holistic and systemic taxonomy that categorizes methods along task integration, tracking formulation, and representation flow. We define three paradigms -Early, Late, and Full Unified Perception- and systematically review existing methods, their architectures, training strategies, datasets used, and open-source availability, while highlighting future research directions. This work establishes the first comprehensive framework for understanding and advancing unified perception, consolidates fragmented efforts, and guides future research toward more robust, generalizable, and interpretable perception.
♻ ☆ WM-VS: Progress-Aligned World Models for Closed-Loop Visual Servoing
Guanzhong Sun, Junyi Ma, Yixuan Zhou, Yuxuan Wu, Yanzi Miao, Hesheng Wang
Closed-loop visual servoing requires predictions that indicate whether an action reduces task error, not only whether the action is plausible. We call this gap the prediction-control mismatch and introduce WM-VS, a target-centric progress-aligned world-model framework for closed-loop visual servoing. Offline target-region DINOv2 correspondences define a signed four-dimensional servo coordinate for translation, scale, and in-plane rotation. Stage 1 aligns action-conditioned latent transitions with this coordinate; Stage 2 freezes the world model and trains a reactive joint-velocity policy with action imitation, consequence supervision, and short imagined rollouts that favor error contraction. Deployment is RGB-only and reactive, without online trajectory optimization. On a real 7-DoF eye-to-hand system, WM-VS reaches a corner RMSE no larger than 10 percent of its initial value in 30/30 trials and retains this criterion at the final valid frame in 25/30 (83.33 percent). Removing future-error alignment reduces retention to 26.67 percent. The learned progress signal agrees with an external AprilTag corner error not used for training or control (mean Spearman rho = 0.8778). Without retraining, two unseen 3D targets achieve translation-error reductions of 86.48 percent and 90.27 percent and rotation-error reductions of 70.01 percent and 65.70 percent. These results link progress-aligned action consequences to repeated closed-loop correction and transfer. Code and data will be released as open source.
♻ ☆ Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Models
Lichao Ni, Yuhan Liu, Pengfei Li, Guanghuan Fang
Specialized vision-language-action (VLA) policies acquire strong domain-specific skills, yet consolidating these skills into one shared policy remains challenging. On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher knowledge on inputs induced by the student, addressing the distribution mismatch encountered during deployment. For flow-based VLAs, this mismatch arises at two levels: environment observations and intermediate action-generation states. We propose a two-level on-policy distillation framework that couples student-driven environment interaction with teacher velocity supervision along student-generated action flow trajectories. Frozen domain specialists jointly supervise one student. After each update, the student collects new environment experience and generates fresh action-flow trajectories. Starting from a joint supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization, Velocity Loss OPD yields absolute success-rate gains of 22.55% on LIBERO-40, 33.4% on CALVIN five-instruction sequences, and 22.6% on Meta-World MT50. Compared with Action Loss OPD and Teacher-rollout SFT, it achieves absolute success-rate gains of 6.4-9.5% on LIBERO-40, 9.7-18.3% on CALVIN, and 3.2-4.2% on Meta-World MT50. Analysis by sequence length further shows larger success-rate gains on longer CALVIN sequences. These results demonstrate effective multi-domain capability consolidation through two-level on-policy supervision, with a single student deployed across domains.

♻ ☆ RankFormer: A Propose-then-Select Transformer for Multi-Agent Multimodal Trajectory Prediction
Diyi Liu, Zihan Niu, Tu Xu, Xingchen Zhang, Lishan Sun
Predicting traffic agent trajectories plays an important role in autonomous driving, traffic operations, transportation safety analysis, etc. Although many deep learning algorithms are devised to predict future agent trajectories, the trajectory prediction problem is still challenging due to the complexity of decision-making process, interactions with surrounding vehicles, and the existence of multiple possible intentions for the traveling agents even under similar scenarios. Most existing methods are limited by the requirement of graph structures (e.g., Graph Neural Network) or the requirement of manually labeled intentions. In this study, we propose a pure Transformer-based deep learning model for multi-modal trajectory prediction considering temporal dependencies and agent-agent spatial interactions. After encoding the historical trajectories, two parallel decoders are employed to generate trajectories and probabilities on separate decoder tracks. The model is evaluated on two real-world datasets, one highway dataset and the other pedestrian dataset with solid performance. One important insight is that following a ``propose-then-select'' strategy, the agent-agent spatial interactions are only considered for probability estimation instead of trajectory generation. In summary, the proposed model provides a potential direction to design more robust and effective multi-modal trajectory prediction models.

♻ ☆ Neural 3D Object Reconstruction with Small-Scale Unmanned Aerial Vehicles
Àlmos Veres-Vitàlyos, Filip Lemic, Daniel Johannes Bugelnig, Joan Bernaus Casadesús, Genis Castillo Gomez-Raya, Sergi Abadal, Bernhard Rinner, Xavier Costa-Pérez
Miniaturized Uncrewed Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) can access indoor and hard-to-reach spaces, but severe constraints on payload and autonomy have limited their use in demanding tasks such as high-quality 3D reconstruction. We introduce a novel system architecture that enables autonomous, high-fidelity 3D scanning of static objects with sub-100 gram UAVs. Our core innovation lies in a closed-loop active viewpoint selection framework specifically tailored for ultra-constrained micro-platforms, advancing beyond standard static or offline active reconstruction methods. The framework establishes a dual-reconstruction pipeline that creates a real-time (RT) feedback loop between data capture and flight control. A near-RT process uses Structure-from-Motion (SfM) to generate an instantaneous point-cloud of the object. A systematic trajectory adaptation algorithm analyzes the model quality on the fly and dynamically adapts the UAV's trajectory based on parameterized spatial partitioning to intelligently capture new images of poorly covered areas, ensuring comprehensive acquisition. For the final, high-fidelity output, a non-RT pipeline employs a Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)-based Neural 3D Reconstruction (N3DR) approach, fusing SfM-derived camera poses with precise external location data, evaluated across both radio-based Ultra Wideband (UWB) and visual motion-capture setups, to correct sensor noise and achieve superior accuracy. We implemented and validated this architecture using Crazyflie 2.1 UAVs. Our experiments, conducted in both single- and multi-UAV configurations show that algorithmic dynamic trajectory adaptation consistently improves reconstruction quality over static flight paths. This work demonstrates a scalable and autonomous solution that unlocks the potential of miniaturized UAVs for fine-grained 3D reconstruction, a capability previously reserved for much larger platforms.

♻ ☆ Stubborn: A Streamlined and Unified Reinforcement Learning Framework for Robust Motion Tracking and Fall Recovery for Humanoids
Yuhui Yang, Xiao Ren, Zongbiao Weng, Zhijie Liu, He Kong
Recent reinforcement learning approaches have shown great promise in improving humanoid motion tracking performance and achieving fall recovery under disturbances. However, most existing works treat motion tracking and fall recovery as different tasks and require multi-stage training with specialized recovery rewards and/or separate recovery policies. Moreover, existing reinforcement learning-based methods often terminate training episodes immediately after severe tracking failures, limiting recovery-oriented exploration in unstable or fallen states. To address the above issues, we propose Stubborn, a streamlined and unified reinforcement learning framework to achieve robust humanoid motion tracking and fall recovery. Specifically, Stubborn uses an asymmetric Actor-Critic architecture and consists of three major components. First, a yaw-aligned tracking representation is adopted to reduce sensitivity to global drift and heading disturbances while preserving gravity-related balance information. Second, we introduce a Bernoulli-based probabilistic termination mechanism that enables the policy to encourage exploration of fall-recovery behaviors under varying failure modes. Third, we propose a probabilistic termination and tracking-error-driven strategy that dynamically reshapes the sampling distribution based on tracking performance, increasing the training efficiency for difficult motion segments and unstable states. Extensive comparisons with SOTA methods and ablation studies show that Stubborn achieved competitive performance and avoided the reward-hacking tendency of baseline methods, and the proposed probabilistic termination mechanism and adaptive sampling strategy contributed to the performance and robustness gains. For real-world demonstrations, please refer to the project page at https://aislab-sustech.github.io/Stubborn/.
comment: Project page at https://aislab-sustech.github.io/Stubborn/
♻ ☆ StereoVLM: Binocular Vision-Language Models for Metric 3D Spatial Reasoning
Chi Yan, Guoyang Zhao, Wentao Yuan, Yixiao Ge, Yanning Zhou, Dan Xu
Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations. To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning. StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. We further find that disparity supervision generalizes substantially better than direct binocular depth supervision on unseen environments. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark across three levels, from point-level geometry to object-level spatial reasoning. StereoVLM-8B achieves 95.17% depth accuracy ($δ_1$) and a 66.98 average object-level score on Stereo3D-Bench. Intervention results further indicate that the model's performance on Stereo3D-Bench benefits from valid cross-view geometry and cannot be explained solely by additional visual tokens or semantic priors. Hierarchical geometric supervision also yields average gains of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points in RoboCasa manipulation success.
comment: Project page: https://xpeng-robotics.github.io/stereovlm/
♻ ☆ From Predictive Geometry to Action: Learning Complementary Predictive Representations for Embodied Manipulation
Xiaoxu Xu, Hao Li, Hongtao Zhang, Yili Tang, Jiafei Cao, Junhao Cai, Haoxiang Ma, Weixin Li, Weinan Zhang
Effective manipulation requires a policy to capture not only about the current scene geometry, but also about how that geometry will evolve under interaction. Existing approaches either augment policies with geometric information from current observations or introduce future prediction as auxiliary supervision, leaving open how predictive geometry should be represented for action generation. Therefore, we propose a two-stage framework, which learns complementary predictive representations from multi-view video clips. During pretraining, a frozen 3D foundation model provides dense geometric features that are compressed into predictive geometric representations and optimized to preserve scene structure and its temporal evolution. Action supervision is then applied to geometric transitions to extract a complementary motor representation that emphasizes action-relevant transitions. During downstream post-training, predictive geometry is transferred through geometry queries, while the motor representation guides intermediate features along the action-generation pathway. Future observations are used only as privileged supervision during training and are not required at inference time. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, SimplerEnv, and real-world bimanual and single-arm tasks, our approach consistently improves downstream policies, including an absolute gain of 10.4 percentage points on the WidowX evaluation. We further demonstrate transfer across multiple VLA architectures and WAMs, with improvements in both future-world and action prediction. The code will be available at https://github.com/xuxiaoxxxx/CPR.
♻ ☆ RoboColiseum: Co-evolution of Simulation, Evaluation, and Models
Chenghao Yin, Da Huang, Di Yang, Jichao Wang, Junhui Wu, Nanshu Zhao, Tong Ran, Zhijun Li, Gang Zhao, Linting Guo, Rui Feng, Sheng Zhang, Tianyu Jiang, Wenjun Sun, Yongxin Su, Zhaobo Liu, Zheyuan Xing, Sukai Wang, Yue Zhou, Qihan Jiang, Jianhua Jiang, Chuang Men, Yuxiang Yan, Daizhen Lv, Kunyu Yu, Yongjian Shen, Tianxiang Zhu, Siying Zhang, Wenhao Wang, Jun Zhao, Bowen Jiang, Zhi Zeng, Maoqing Yao, Qian Wang
Simulation-based evaluation of embodied models requires calibrated interactions, diverse tasks, and explicit execution constraints. We present RoboColiseum, a platform combining system identification, composable physics and rendering, and multidimensional benchmarking. Recorded-command replay characterizes robot dynamics and object interactions, while a shared interface connects rigid and deformable simulation to rendering. Across 22 paired real--simulation robot--task configurations, task scores have a reported Pearson correlation of 0.9686. Eight evaluation tracks span instruction following, spatial reasoning, general manipulation, robustness, dexterous manipulation, precision manipulation, whole-body coordination, and execution across robot embodiments. Budget-aware scoring combines task progress, resource use, and completion rewards. We report 12 selected Season~I policies and all 11 systems on the public Season~II leaderboard, comprising eight Agent systems and three VLA policies. Agent2Act connects language models to robot-control execution; the VLA study uses mixed-task supervised fine-tuning. The results reveal substantial variation across tracks within each evaluation category. RoboColiseum connects simulation development with capability-oriented evaluation and provides a foundation for extending robot interactions and model assessment.
comment: 11 pages, 8 figures. The first eight authors contributed equally. Maoqing Yao and Qian Wang are the corresponding authors
♻ ☆ Tripwire: Robot Agents that Program Their Own Interrupts under Human Disturbance
Sunli Chen, Yun Zong, Qinhong Zhou, Xiaowen Qiu, Jiaben Chen, Zeyuan Yang, Chuang Gan
Agent harnesses are turn-based: the agent acts, waits for the result, then reasons. When the action invokes a pretrained robot policy, such as a vision-language-action (VLA) or world action model (WAM), the policy may react continuously to observations, but the agent cannot revisit its decision until the call returns. Meanwhile, a person may step into the robot's path or move the object it is about to grasp. Invoking the agent more often narrows this blind interval, but a reasoning model takes seconds per decision and most control steps need no new one. We propose TRIP, a training-free, event-driven harness in which the agent programs its own interrupts. With each call, the agent writes a tripwire: a lightweight, stateful Python program that runs alongside the policy, can query a compact VLM (for example, to locate a person and measure their distance), and decides whether the call continues or control returns to the agent. When it fires, the harness halts the policy and returns control with the reason; the agent then reassesses, adapts, and continues under a rewritten tripwire. We evaluate TRIP with three VLAs and one WAM on RoboHD, a benchmark of 168 RoboCasa365 scenes in which a simulated person disturbs the robot and any human-robot contact counts as failure. Compared with a turn-based harness using the same agent and tools, TRIP halves the rate of human contact with the strongest policy, raising safety from 61.3% to 81.3%, without sacrificing task success (38.7% vs. 31.0%). Real-robot experiments show that TRIP completes two manipulation tasks under human interference where the turn-based harness and the policy alone largely fail.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition 100
☆ Pruning Autonomous Driving VLAs: What to Preserve for Reasoning and Action
Seongchan Kim, Soowon Son, Sangoh Kim, Hyunah Ko, Eunbeen Hong, Hyunkoo Lee, Sanghyun Lee, WonJun Moon, Kihong Kim, Dongyeon Son, Woongchan Nam, Seungryong Kim
Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models for autonomous driving use chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to guide action generation, but incur substantial memory and computational costs. We study structured pruning for these models, focusing on preserving both scene understanding and trajectory prediction. Our analysis of Taylor importance in Alpamayo-1.5-10B shows that reasoning and trajectory objectives assign different importance to the same vision-language model (VLM) structures. In the action expert, MLP channels exhibit more stable importance rankings across denoising steps than query heads, and a small fraction of channels accounts for most of the measured importance. Based on these findings, we propose MoOP, which combines importance ranks from both objectives for VLM pruning and aggregates stepwise importance to select a fixed subset of expert MLP channels. At 24.0% total parameter reduction, VLM-only pruning with MoOP performs comparably to or slightly better than the strongest baselines in driving, while retaining 94.0% of the dense model's LingoQA score, far above all other methods. At a higher reduction of 30.0%, MoOP degrades much less than every other method, as it is the only one whose reasoning does not collapse. Removing 93.75% of expert MLP channels increases total parameter reduction to 39.4%, with nearly unchanged open-loop errors relative to VLM-only pruning and competitive closed-loop performance. The resulting model achieves a 1.37x end-to-end inference speedup and 36.6% lower peak memory than the dense model, without post-pruning fine-tuning.

☆ Lyris: Layout-Guided Long Video Generation with Persistent 3D Memory
Chen Wang, Jiahui Huang, Riccardo de Lutio, Alex Trevithick, Bryan Chu, Jiawei Ren, Laura Leal-Taixé, Shengyu Huang, Lingjie Liu, Haithem Turki
Exploring a scene from as little as a single photo requires generating a long, camera-controlled walkthrough that extends far beyond what was captured, yet remains consistent upon return. Memory-based video generation methods preserve what they have already seen, but have no anchor beyond it, where the camera drifts from its path and a text prompt can name objects but not place them. Layout-conditioned methods provide such an anchor and precise control over what appears where, but rely on layouts that are typically authored by hand. Both limitations arise because, beyond what was captured, nothing anchors the video model unless a human authors one. To overcome both, we propose Lyris, a long video generation framework that never leaves the video model without an anchor: a persistent point-cloud memory where the scene has been observed or generated, and a 3D layout that a vision-language model authors where it has not. Our key insight is that the interface between the two models can be surprisingly coarse. A layout of one labeled 3D box per object is simple enough for a vision-language model to author (and for a user to edit), yet expressive enough for a video model to follow once rendered along the camera path. We demonstrate walkthroughs of over three minutes and 50 meters from a single photo, passing through doorways into rooms it never shows. When evaluated on minute-long round trips across four datasets, Lyris outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a wide margin, reducing camera error by 3.8x and improving consistency upon return by 22% on average.
comment: Project page: http://research.nvidia.com/labs/sil/projects/lyris
☆ Modern Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Are Pareidolic
Zihang Lin, Huaiyuan Qin, Liangli Zhen, Qing Guo, Jun Liu, Yew-Soon Ong, Hongyuan Zhu
In human perception, pareidolia is the tendency to perceive a meaningful pattern, such as a face, in a random or ambiguous stimulus.We find a similar phenomenon in modern self-supervised Vision Transformers (ViTs): on white noise, which contains neither objects nor spatial structure, a few directions of their features still form spatially coherent patterns across the patches, imposed by the features themselves.We call this behavior pareidolia, and the span of these directions the pareidolic subspace.On natural images, it holds most of the feature variance in DINOv2 and DINOv3 but little in DINO.This excess explains why DINOv2 and DINOv3, despite stronger dense features, fall far behind DINO in object emergence, the hallmark ability of self-supervised ViTs to identify the patches of an object on their own.Our experiments further show that scaling down their pareidolic subspaces steadily restores their ability to discover objects, so their object emergence is hindered rather than lost.These findings naturally lead to a training-free calibration: Pareidolia Subspace Calibration(PSC) measures the pareidolic subspace only on a noise input and then calibrates the features of natural inputs by scaling its directions down to the variance level of the remaining directions.Across diverse object emergence tasks, PSC improves DINOv2 and DINOv3 by up to 31.7 CorLoc on object discovery, 30.2 maxF on saliency detection and 59.9~$\mathcal{J}$ on video object segmentation.To identify the cause of pareidolia, we trace it block by block and find that it forms in the middle blocks of every self-supervised model we examine but stays strong to the last block only in models trained with a patch-level loss; controlled training confirms that an image-level loss alone lets it fade.
☆ Let Vision-Language Models Generate Images through Their Representations
JB Kim, Byungwoo Jeon, Kyungmin Lee, Hyeonmo Kang, Cheonbok Park, Shinyoung Joo, Jinwoo Shin, Jeonghoon Kim
Recent unified multimodal models aim to combine visual understanding and generation within a single model, yet effectively integrating the two capabilities remains challenging. Leveraging pretrained vision-language models offers a way to build on already learned multimodal knowledge, but making this knowledge effectively accessible to visual generation remains nontrivial. We find that a central challenge lies in the heterogeneous visual representations used for understanding and generation. To address this challenge, we introduce Integral, which converts a pretrained vision-language model into a unified multimodal model by constructing a shared visual representation space across the two capabilities. Integral implements this design through two complementary components. Abstraction Fusion constructs shared visual tokens by aggregating hierarchical representations from the frozen vision encoder, while Block-wise MoT introduces a lightweight generative stream that interacts with the vision-language model only at block boundaries. Our approach effectively preserves the pretrained understanding capability while extending it to strong visual generation. Controlled comparisons further demonstrate that sharing visual representations between understanding and generation substantially improves generative learning compared with using a separate visual representation space, despite comparable reconstruction fidelity. These results suggest that representations learned by pretrained vision-language models already provide an effective foundation for visual generation.
comment: Preprint. Project page: https://thejb.ai/integral
☆ TowerBridge: Bridging the Dual-Encoder Modality Gap via Weight-Space Programming
Hani Alomari, Md Atabuzzaman, Chris Thomas
CLIP-style dual encoders map images and text through two separate towers into a shared embedding space, where the two modalities occupy distinct regions separated by a modality gap. Retrieval fails when wrong matches, or hard negatives, outrank the correct one, and the gap is the usual suspect. Yet removing it post hoc degrades retrieval on every CLIP checkpoint we test. We introduce a paired statistic that identifies directions where the two towers agree more on hard negatives than on matched pairs. Mildly attenuating these directions improves retrieval while largely preserving the gap. We arrive at this correction through weight-space programming: guided by the statistic, an LLM agent inspects both towers and writes closed-form weight edits without backpropagation. Free to edit any component, the agent improves COCO test retrieval on all 13 CLIP checkpoints and edits an output projection in 12 of the 13. We distill and refine its recurring correction into TowerBridge, a closed-form recipe motivated by a first-order analysis of the hard-negative margin. Computed in seconds from 25,000 labelled pairs, it requires no model-specific tuning and leaves the architecture and inference cost unchanged. TowerBridge improves COCO test retrieval by 16.8 RSUM and Flickr30k test retrieval by 6.6 on average across all 21 evaluated CLIP checkpoints, including 8 unseen by the agent, while limiting any drop in ImageNet zero-shot accuracy to 0.5 points. It also reduces hubness on all 21 checkpoints and improves retrieval on 4 of 5 dual encoders from other families.

☆ Self-Supervised Dataset Distillation via Mutual Information Maximization
Mohammad Hossein Moslemi, Mahdi Beitollahi, Zhimin Mei, Jiale Cai, Bissan Ghaddar, Boyu Wang
Dataset distillation (DD) aims to compress a large dataset into a small synthetic one that remains effective for training neural networks. Despite its success in supervised learning, DD remains underexplored in self-supervised learning (SSL), where distilled data must preserve the information needed to learn representations that remain consistent across augmentations. To bridge this gap, we introduce Mutual Information Prototype Alignment (MIPA), an efficient SSL dataset distillation approach that optimizes synthetic images to preserve augmentation-invariant information. Specifically, MIPA treats synthetic images as learnable prototypes and uses a frozen encoder to assign real samples to them based on feature similarity. A synthetic dataset that preserves such augmentation invariance should yield stable prototype assignments across multiple augmented views of the same real image. MIPA encourages this by maximizing mutual information between cross-view assignments while avoiding trivial solutions in which all real samples are assigned to only a few synthetic prototypes. Evaluations on image classification benchmarks show that synthetic data generated by MIPA yield higher-quality representations than existing distillation approaches while reducing time and storage demands during distillation.

Mohammed Baharoon, Sung Eun Kim, Mahmoud Hussain Alabbad, Lucas Bijnens, Ali Piracha, Reem Alwasiah, Talal Yahyan, Abdulrahman Alamoudi, Mashael Alshehri, Rayan Alsager, Hannah Hancock, Anna M. Hunkemöller, Peter Youssef, Mona A. Alhammad, Afnan Aljumayan, Brecht Van Berkel, Eric Bijnens, Saud Alhussain, Maarten Steyvers, Rolf Symons, Bryan Eelen, Ayed Alaklubi, Maha Buraykan Alshammari, Amirah Fahad Alshammeri, Tomas Gilvydis, Ibrahim AlTurki, Monerah Almohideb, Ali Alburkani, Shahad Alhomaiani, Fatima Jabali, Abdulrhman Aljouie, Daesung Kim, Junha Im, Michael Moritz, Hassan R. Alomaish, Pranav Rajpurkar
Radiology reports describe findings in text only, without visually marking them on the scan, so readers cannot directly see which abnormality each reported finding refers to. We introduce CTLink, a text-prompted 3D segmentation model that segments findings described in a chest CT report. CTLink was trained on 4123 noncontrast chest CT scans with 9547 segmented report findings, including ReXGroundingCTv2, a newly annotated dataset of 1134 scans and 1895 findings with every instance of each finding segmented. On the 200 ReXGroundingCT validation scans, CTLink achieved a hit rate of 0.816, an instance F1 score of 0.456, and a mean Dice score of 0.400, compared with 0.533, 0.175, and 0.234 for VoxTell, a publicly available text-prompted segmentation model (P < .001 for all). On the test set of the MICCAI 2026 ReXGrounding challenge, an ensemble of seven CTLink models achieved the highest hit rate (0.782) and instance F1 score (0.386) of all 48 participating teams. On 50 test scans segmented twice by independent radiologists, CTLink matched or exceeded inter-rater agreement. Diffuse non-focal findings remained the main limitation, partly because their extent is outlined inconsistently even between radiologists. The CTLink model weights are available at https://huggingface.co/rajpurkarlab/CTLink, and the dataset at https://huggingface.co/datasets/rajpurkarlab/ReXGroundingCT.

☆ LeJEPA Features Are Not Isotropic, and Should Not Be
Richeek Das, Pratik Chaudhari
The SIGReg term in LeJEPA regularizes features to have an isotropic Gaussian distribution. Our first result is to show that this regularizer, in practice, cannot achieve its goal. We design a modified regularizer to enforce the objective better. This leads to slightly improved performance. For example, on ImageNet-100, our modified regularizer reaches the final accuracy of SIGReg in 1.3$\times$ fewer epochs. Our second result argues that self-supervised encoders should not have isotropic Gaussian features. We show that the alignment term in LeJEPA conflicts with SIGReg, because it couples the magnitude of the features with their directions. In contrast, isotropic Gaussian features would entail independent magnitude and directions. Features obtained with LeJEPA are, in fact, not isotropic. So LeJEPA has two issues. Its regularizer is weak, and the isotropic Gaussian target is too strict. Our third result is about reformulating the isotropic Gaussian regularizer to enforce only the marginal distributions of the magnitude and direction, without enforcing independence. This leads to a simple regularization term, PolarReg, that can be optimized reliably across many different datasets, batch sizes and embedding dimensions without any hyper-parameter changes. On ImageNet-1k, our technique matches the accuracy of LeJEPA and its variants in 4.7$\times$ fewer epochs. It improves the final accuracy by 1.8 points.
☆ WorldLatent: A Unified 4D Latent Space for World Perception and Generation
Jingxi Chen, Yujia Chen, Cornelia Fermuller, Yiannis Aloimonos, Wen-Sheng Chu, Du Tran
Generative Pre-Training (GPT) represents a profound milestone in natural language processing, serving as the foundation for most of today's state-of-the-art large language models. By casting diverse understanding and generation problems into a shared token representation, GPT enables a single architecture and unified optimization loop to master heterogeneous tasks across massive corpora, giving rise to powerful foundation models for natural language. In contrast, 4D spatiotemporal vision lacks a common representational protocol: perception (such as depth and camera estimation) and generation are either handled by separate one-way pipelines or bolted together from unaligned single-modality spaces. In this work, we introduce WorldLatent, a framework that formulates a unified 4D latent space as a common protocol for both world perception and generation. Rather than relying on fragmented, task-specific models or stacked single-modality representations, our framework proposes a multimodal VAE architecture that compresses and fuses complex 4D visual appearance, geometry, and dynamics into a single structured latent representation. Within this formulation, perception and generation operate as complementary denoising processes over the same latent space, enabling one generative model to learn both capabilities simultaneously within a single training loop. Experiments across representative 4D benchmarks verify that our fused latent protocol achieves specialist-level zero-shot 4D perception, coherent 4D generation, and controllable editing from a single model. By demonstrating that diverse 4D tasks can be seamlessly unified under a shared representational protocol, our work provides a scalable foundation for general-purpose 4D spatial intelligence.

Recent multimodal search agents use reasoning, vision, and live web search across many turns to answer questions beyond parametric knowledge by orchestrating a small library of hand-crafted search and visual tools. However, the library is laborious to create and maintain, and frozen when new query types, evidence formats, and failure modes are encountered in the wild. Human practitioners, by contrast, cope with insufficient tools by fashioning new ones from familiar parts and reusing them across tasks. Inspired by this, we propose ToolSmith, an automatic tool-generation framework that grows and reuses modules on top of a lean base tool library. We evaluate ToolSmith on three in-domain multimodal search benchmarks and ten out-of-domain benchmarks under a VLM-as-a-Judge protocol. ToolSmith consistently improves over the base library across deployed agents of varying scales, with larger backbones reaping greater gains, demonstrating the scalability of the approach. Our code and data are available at https://threesr.github.io/toolsmith/.
☆ On-Policy Codec Distillation for Efficient All-in-One Video Generation
Boyang Wang, Kevin Blackburn-Matzen, Oindrila Saha, Matheus Gadelha, Zezhou Cheng
Modern visual generative models operate on tokens, and every visual asset they receive, whether an identity, a scribble, a depth map, or a motion video, is tokenized and appended to the input token sequence. Consequently, conditioning quickly dominates the computation cost. Yet most of these tokens carry redundant spatiotemporal information. Our key insight is that identifying what is genuinely new is exactly the problem that classical video codecs have long solved. Thus, we first introduce a codec-based token pruning method that discards redundant tokens. Then, we propose an on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) strategy to train a DiT adapter capable of learning the codec pruning pattern well without quality degradation. Together, they form On-Policy Codec Distillation (CodecOPSD). We scale CodecOPSD to 16 condition modalities on our own video diffusion model, where it prunes 66% of the condition tokens on average with almost no quality drop. Therefore, denoising becomes 2x faster, and the cache memory shrinks by up to 73% in KV cache mode. CodecOPSD also extends to other state-of-the-art pretrained image and video generative models, where its benefit grows further with more conditions, longer frames, and higher resolution.
