☆ Spatiotemporal Graph Neural Networks for Fault Detection and Structural Learning in Chemical Processes: Use Case on the Tennessee Eastman Process
Rayane Ammar Khodja, Alexandre Voisin, Victor Costa, Fanny Casteran, Benoit Celse, Benoît Iung
Classical Fault Detection and Diagnosis (FDD) methods, including many data-driven approaches, assume a static normal operating space and interpret deviations from a fixed reference as fault indicators. When Operating Conditions (OCs) vary over time, this assumption breaks down: legitimate transitions trigger false alarms while moderate faults go undetected. We propose a spatiotemporal Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework that decomposes the normal operating space into OC-specific subspaces linked by transition functions, with a dual learning objective combining reconstruction loss and a Deep SVDD one-class term. It learns adjacency matrices through Graph Attention Networks (GATs) and integrates spatial modelling with temporal encoding to represent process dynamics under evolving OCs. This paper evaluates the framework's foundational components (fault detection, GATv2 spatial graph learning and temporal encoding) on the Tennessee Eastman Process (TEP) benchmark, training only on fault-free data. The architecture achieves competitive detection from reconstruction error alone, with similarity-based feature selection improving both accuracy and graph structure diversity. We then evaluate the physical interpretability of the learned attention matrices against 22 ground-truth sensor pairs derived from the TEP control structure and process topology. GATv2 attention fails to recover all known physical pairs across multiple hyperparameter configurations, suggesting a structural limitation of reconstruction-driven attention rather than a tuning issue. This challenges a common assumption in GNN-based FDD: that learned attention weights provide a basis for fault diagnosis and root-cause analysis. The architecture detects faults effectively, but the learned graph does not encode the physical topology needed for interpretable diagnosis, motivating physics-informed graph construction.

Manh V. Nguyen, Liang Zhao, Bobin Deng, Xinyue Zhang, Shaoen Wu
Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), widely regarded as the third generation of neural networks, represent a promising neuromorphic computing paradigm with the potential to reduce the energy footprint of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Their en-ergy efficiency makes SNNs particularly attractive for resource-constrained Edge AI devices, motivating growing research interest in Federated Learning (FL) with SNNs. Despite these advantages, integrating SNNs into existing FL systems remains challenging, as replacing all conventional Artificial Neural Network (ANN) devices with SNN-based alternatives is impractical. Instead, we envision a gradual transition toward neuromorphic Edge AI, where ANN and SNN devices coexist and collaboratively participate in FL. To facilitate this transition, we propose Hybrid Neuromorphic Federated Learning (HNFL), a framework that enables joint training of heterogeneous ANN and SNN devices within an FL environment. Through experiments on CIFAR-10 using both VGG9 and ResNet architectures, we demonstrate the mutual benefits of collaborative ANN-SNN training. Specifically, HNFL achieves an average improvement of 16.85% when incorporating SNN devices into ANN-based FL and 8.02% when incorporating ANN devices into SNN-based FL. Furthermore, HNFL produces sparser spiking activity in the trained SNN models, with reductions of 12.4% for SResNet and 22.4% for SVGG9. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to demonstrate that ANNs and SNNs can coexist and mutually benefit from collaborative training in FL, providing a practical path toward the gradual integration of neuromorphic computing into existing Edge AI systems.

In transformer segmentation models, attention is usually visualized after training rather than supervised. Although attention supervision has been explored for natural images and driving scenes, aerial forest segmentation typically uses attention only as an architectural component and evaluates interpretability qualitatively. We present CanopyFormer, an attention-guided SegFormer-B0 that uses an Attention Consistency Loss to align attention with the ground-truth forest mask, encouraging attention to focus on canopy regions. Since SegFormer uses spatial-reduction attention, we adapt Gradient-weighted Attention Rollout by restricting it to the final encoder stage, where the attention matrix is square. We introduce Average Attention-Mask Overlap (AAMO) to measure attention alignment and incorporate a deletion test to evaluate faithfulness. On 5108 images, our method increases AAMO from 0.0334 to 0.7476, approximately 22 times the vanilla SegFormer-B0 result, with a modest decrease in Dice score from 0.8743 to 0.8577. The deletion test reveals that improved alignment does not necessarily translate into improved faithfulness: removing the most-attended 25% of patches reduces the forest score by 12.1%, compared with 33.0% when removing random patches. Attention supervision introduces no additional inference cost, although double backpropagation makes each training step 2.6 to 2.8 times slower. The attention alignment improvement also generalizes to a second dataset, LoveDA. Additionally, a Boundary Refinement Module provides no consistent Dice improvement and reduces AAMO, while mean squared error substantially outperforms Kullback-Leibler divergence as the attention loss.

☆ Can pretrained Transformers deliver semiparametrically efficient inference?
Han Yan, Jin Zhu, Chengchun Shi, Tengyao Wang
Semiparametric models provide a broad framework for statistical inference, yet efficient estimation typically relies on influence function correction tailored to each estimand and on nuisance estimation repeated for every sample. We show that a single pretrained Transformer can deliver efficient estimation and valid inference for a family of estimands in one forward pass, without deriving efficient influence functions or estimating nuisance functions. Pretrained on simulated data with the true parameter as the only label, the Transformer learns the posterior mean and covariance of the queried estimand and hence returns an estimate and a Wald-type confidence region. Theoretically, we prove that, for locally flat pretraining priors of slowly growing complexity, the posterior mean is efficient for every queried estimand. The Transformer inherits this efficiency with asymptotically exact coverage, in probability over evaluation populations and queries, even under distribution shift. We also reveal that the guarantee places much higher demands on pretraining when the data-generating distribution is fixed, as in classical frequentist inference. Experiments on causal inference, partial linear regression, and survival analysis show that the pretrained model generally achieves the lowest estimation error among competing methods, with nearly nominal coverage, at a computational cost of only about 0.02 seconds per dataset.

Existing approaches often overlook evolving user behavior, introduce semantic noise by ignoring user stance, and fail to handle newly emerging users effectively. To address these limitations, we propose a \underline{S}emantic \underline{M}isinformation \underline{S}preader \underline{D}etection approach (SMSD) that models misinformation propagation as a temporal, user-centric, and behavior-driven learning problem. A stance-aware labeling strategy is also introduced to differentiate supportive, opposing, questioning, and neutral users towards misinformation claims. Additionally, a monthly quantile analysis is introduced to simulate realistic, evolving user participation. Initial experimental results on the FibVid COVID-19 benchmark dataset demonstrate that SMSD improves recall by 45.0\%, F1 by 49.5\%, and MCC by 74.6\% under stance-aware labeling and by 17.7\%, 7.4\%, and 11.4\%, respectively, under threshold-based labeling. Data selection has emerged as an effective approach to reducing the model training costs. However, most existing methods often rely heavily on sample hardness, which may overlook differences in sample learning dynamics and lead to suboptimal sample selection. In this paper, we propose LeDAS, an end-to-end Learning Dynamics-Aware Selection framework for dynamic data selection, which jointly characterizes sample importance through hardness, learning progress, and deterioration, enabling adaptive sample prioritization throughout training with marginal additional computational overhead. Furthermore, a bounded staleness compensation mechanism accounts for historical selection patterns by increasing the selection priority of samples that have not been selected for extended periods. Extensive experiments across diverse vision and language tasks demonstrate the effectiveness and generality of LeDAS. Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, LeDAS consistently achieves superior performance, matching or surpassing full-dataset training at a 50\% selection ratio on ImageNet-1K and in LLM supervised fine-tuning. Moreover, its modular and task-agnostic design enables the integration of complementary selection signals, demonstrating strong robustness to noisy and corrupted datasets.

☆ Late-Time Dynamics of Flow Matching: Distance Geometry and Learning
Umberto Biccari, Junqing Huang, Kang Liu, Enrique Zuazua
Generative models transform simple random inputs into samples that resemble observed data. For a finite training set, a central question is how its geometry shapes the terminal dynamics and the probabilities assigned to individual samples. We address this question for flow matching with linear interpolation between independent Gaussian and empirical samples. The squared distance to the training set generates explicit paths contracting exponentially toward the nearest sample. We prove that exact trajectories restarted at prescribed late-time states approximate these paths uniformly over all elapsed times and compact sets of starting states away from Voronoi interfaces, with an error exponentially small in the inverse squared restart noise scale. The initial mass near interfaces controls the quadratic Wasserstein error between the exact and reference laws. For Gaussian and fixed Gaussian-tube restart laws, this gives a square-root rate in the restart noise scale, uniform over time, which a two-site example shows to be sharp in general. At ties, the Clarke subdifferential characterizes the graphical limit of the rescaled velocity field. This geometry motivates two learning methods: fitting the distance potential with value and gradient supervision, and fitting velocities along explicit contraction paths. A transport estimate separates initialization mismatch, velocity error, incomplete contraction, and endpoint allocation. MNIST experiments illustrate the distinct roles of support proximity, nearest-site retention, and feature fidelity. These results connect flow matching and score-based diffusion through a common limiting geometry and show how asymptotic analysis can inform the design and evaluation of generative models.

However, existing VLA-MBRL methods primarily rely on large-scale image or video generation world models, incurring large computational overhead. This leaves open whether generated sequences are temporally coherent or merely independently plausible, a gap that matters increasingly for sub-daily resolutions since downstream impacts depend on accumulation and persistence, not just on isolated states. This study asks whether autoregressive conditioning can deliver coherent rollouts without error accumulation and ensemble-spread collapse, and whether a single model can expose the resulting coherence-diversity trade-off as a controllable inference choice rather than a fixed design commitment. The noise parameter traces a smooth interpolation between ICON's autocorrelation and PTI generation. AR rollouts of up to six months show no progressive degradation, with ensemble spread contracting only slightly within the first 24 hours. In contrast, the same architecture trained on noise-free previous states diverges. For precipitation PTI underestimates maxima by up to 2x in daily aggregations, while AR tracks ICON's maxima closely. For temperature, differences between modes are negligible. There has been significant recent interest in understanding the behaviour of LLM agents from the perspective of human preferences or corpus statistics. In this paper we propose agent states as intermediate variables through which post-training can be measured and predicted. ☆ Circular Predictive Coding Unlocks Effective Depth
Tommaso Salvatori, Matteo Forasassi
Predictive coding networks perform credit assignment through an energy minimization process. Despite their ability to train models with arbitrary network topologies, they have mostly been used to train feedforward architectures to match the performance of backpropagation. However, they fail to do so when the models become too deep, because error signals become unstable or vanish as they travel through many layers. We address this limitation with circular networks, which get their depth directly from the energy minimization, rather than from stacking layers. Formally, we prove that convergence to an equilibrium of the energy functional of a circular predictive coding network approximates the fixed-point iteration process of a deep equilibrium model, showing that circularity alone suffices to unlock effective depth. Empirically, we show that circular models (i) outperform other predictive coding models of the same size on image classification tasks, matching the accuracy of state-of-the-art predictive coding ResNets and VGG networks despite having substantially fewer parameters; (ii) solve constraint satisfaction problems that require many steps of iterative reasoning, a task not feasible with feedforward models at all, reaching 99.3% test accuracy on Sudoku-hard via nested energy minimization loops; and (iii) scale to autoregressive language modeling by training a circular transformer on TinyStories and WikiText-103, before out of reach for predictive coding models. These results have direct implications for physical neural networks, where computational depth can be traded for recursion on a fixed-size circuit.

Its compositional color-shape benchmark makes forgetting and retained utility measurable from the full output distribution and provides a leave-one-out retraining oracle for each target. From a fixed number of oracle observables, we estimate empirical target coverage, the fraction of targets reliably flagged when deleted and rarely flagged under any other deletions. To recover missed deletions, CEO further expands each observable representation into high-dimensional activation space with the frozen encoder of a SAE trained on the original model. Extensive experiments of 20 baselines shows that even on this simple synthetic task, only retraining from scratch covers all deletion targets.

Replacing the DCNv2 block with DCDN allowed us to eliminate the entire class of manually engineered ratio features from the model input, reducing the number of input features by $40.1\%$. In a live A/B test on this service, DCDN increased likes by $3.25\%$, shares by $16.26\%$, total view time (TVT) by $0.33\%$, and clicks to open fullscreen by $0.38\%$; all changes were statistically significant. In this work, we examine whether different noise instances are equally informative. Using the trained rater to select training noise, we observe three properties of training noise. First, noise realizations at the same timestep are not equally useful: the rater's top-scored noise improves performance over i.i.d. sampling, while its bottom-scored noise degrades it. Second, this utility is contextual: it depends most strongly on the timestep, and to a lesser extent on the image and the class label. Third, noise selection is complementary to timestep-level design, retaining most of its gain when combined with existing scheduling and weighting schemes. Generally, a $c_k\geq0.9$ is needed for an experiment to be sufficiently similar to a target technology. In this work, a physics-informed deep neural network is trained to predict the neutronic sensitivity of grid-based critical experiment geometries. This approach allows for optimization over the combinatorial design space of potential material combinations within the grid, moving beyond traditional parametric optimization approaches. The method is applied to the validation of the TN-Americas TN-LC transportation cask with HALEU fuel, for which existing critical experiment coverage is limited. This application is shown to produce experiment geometries achieving $c_k$ scores of 0.97757, 0.81324, and 0.93276 for three configurations of interest.

Packed dense-angle and re-uploading encodings still live at the fractal q, but not when PCA-95% features are stacked onto those qubits. These results show that output sensitivity is necessary but insufficient: a faithful attribution must control the output through internal computation used for the clean prediction.

The $k$-means++ algorithm chooses its first center uniformly at random from the data points and each subsequent center with probability proportional to its squared distance from the nearest center already chosen. Let $R_k$ be the worst-case ratio between the expected cost of the $k$ seeds chosen by $k$-means++ and the optimal $k$-means cost. In their seminal paper introducing $k$-means++, Arthur and Vassilvitskii (SODA 2007) showed that $2\ln k\le R_k\le8(\ln k+2)$, and Makarychev, Reddy and Shan (NeurIPS 2020) improved the upper bound to $5(\ln k+2)$. We prove that $R_k=2\ln k+O(1)$; more precisely, $2H_{k-1}+2\le R_k\le 2H_{k-2}+5$ for $k\ge2$, where $H_j$ is the $j$th harmonic number, so the two bounds differ by less than $3$. We also determine $R_2=5$ and $R_3=185/32$, with a unified proof of both upper bounds, and give a second family of lower bounds that exceeds $2H_{k-1}+2$ for $2\le k\le18$. Previous analyses bound the expected cost of a cluster just after it is first sampled by a constant times its optimal cost, and then charge that cost for the rest of the run. We track how a cluster's cost evolves after its first hit. At each subsequent draw, the probability of sampling that cluster again is exactly its share of the current cost. ♻ ☆ Finite speed Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-Kac processes and their applications in generative modeling
Richard Duong, Janis Auffenberg, Gabriele Steidl
We study the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-Kac (OU-K) process, where instead of a Brownian motion, a finite-speed Kac process defines the driving process. The OU-K process can be analyzed through a rescaled, time-inhomogeneous Kac process, characterized by a switching rate from the Kac part, and a convergence rate from the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) part. The law of this inhomogeneous Kac process describes the solution of a wave equation, the Euler-Poisson-Darboux (EPD) equation. For Kac switching rates being multiples of the OU convergence rate, we can explicitly derive this EPD solution via the sum of (the derivative of) two Legendre polynomials, restricted between two Dirac points representing the wave fronts. Using the framework of piecewise-deterministic Markov processes (PDMP), we describe the conditional velocity fields of the OU-K process via our polynomial-law-formula. This allows us to apply the OU-K process in a generative flow model. Since the OU-K velocity fields prove to be bounded by the finite Kac speed, the usual time truncations of diffusion models become unnecessary. We demonstrate advantages over diffusion and flow matching models in terms of generation sharpness on singular data sets, while achieving competitive results on CIFAR-10 image generation.

Although compaction is a standard component of coding agent scaffolds, it has not been studied systematically with frontier models on realistic, long horizon agentic tasks. Compaction can, however, silently remove task constraints: on ProgramBench, the first compaction summary already drops about one third of the task's anticheating rules on average, and this rises monotonically with the number of compactions. On real user-agent sessions from SWE-chat, instructions about how the agent should work and what it should not do are dropped around 6 times more than specifications of what to build. We argue that current benchmarks are compaction-friendly: i.e., the objective is fixed and the agent's progress stays on disk, so most of what compaction discards can be recovered, except constraints that don't exist anywhere else.

♻ ☆ Learning to Allocate Resources with Censored Feedback

We study the online resource allocation problem in which at each round, a budget $B$ must be allocated across $K$ arms under censored feedback. An arm yields a reward if and only if two conditions are satisfied: (i) the arm is activated according to an arm-specific Bernoulli random variable with unknown parameter, and (ii) the allocated budget exceeds a random threshold drawn from a parametric distribution with unknown parameter. Over $T$ rounds, the learner must jointly estimate the unknown parameters and allocate the budget so as to maximize cumulative reward facing the exploration-exploitation trade-off. We prove a worst-case regret lower bound $Ω(\sqrt{T})$ for the general model, even with known uniform threshold distributions. We then propose RA-UCB, an optimistic algorithm that leverages non-trivial parameter estimation and confidence bounds. When the budget $B$ is known at the beginning of each round and every arm receives a positive allocation at the optimum (interior optimum, with a known lower bound), RA-UCB achieves a regret bound of order $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$, and even $O(\mathrm{poly}\log T)$ under stronger assumptions. For unknown, round-dependent budgets, we introduce MG-UCB, which allows within-round switching and infinitesimal allocations, and matches the regret guarantees of RA-UCB; we also discuss an implementable discretization. We then validate our theoretical results through experiments on real-world datasets.

But the sensitivity of a unit \textit{saturates} as more units are quantized, so the sum overprices the heavily quantized configurations that tight budgets require. Assuming only that damage accumulates by an associative, increasing, continuous rule restricts it to the form $g\bigl(\sum_i b_i\bigr)$, with summed sensitivities as the case of linear $g$. We propose SaturQ, which uses a concave $g$, fits the per-unit parameters $b_i$ from a single Aumann--Shapley path integral, and allocates formats with a linear program. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, SaturQ lowers KL divergence to BF16 by 11--23\% relative to ModelOpt AutoQuantize at 4.2--6.0 effective bits, and it outperforms an interaction-aware allocator that measures up to 2{,}410 configurations while measuring only three. It also predicts the damage of unmeasured configurations with a median error of 6.9--11.4\%, lower than Gaussian-process and random-forest surrogates fit to 300 configurations, and served allocations of Qwen3.6-27B and GLM-5.2 (753B) run faster than vendor NVFP4 checkpoints at comparable accuracy.

We discuss theoretical bounds for agent-agnostic safety guarantees in environments that can only be partially observed and within which an action is required within limited time. We introduce two realistic scenarios, one with an infinite state space and one with signal mixture. In these scenarios, we prove that even a perfect agent cannot guarantee safe behaviour. It will be argued that for any proof of AI safety or alignment, the environment and associated safe actions need to be specifically considered together with the agent.
♻ ☆ Inpainting physics: self-supervised learning for context-driven fluid simulation
Jonas Weidner, Yeray Martin-Ruisanchez, Daniel Rueckert, Benedikt Wiestler, Julian Suk
Neural surrogate models for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) are typically trained as forward operators that map explicit problem specifications, such as geometry and boundary conditions, to solution fields. This ties the model to the conditioning variables seen during training and limits reuse under boundary-condition shifts or local geometry changes. We propose to reformulate steady CFD inference as an inpainting problem: instead of training on explicit boundary conditions, we learn a self-supervised prior over velocity fields and impose boundary constraints only during inference by fixing known regions such as inlet, outlet or unchanged regions from previous simulations. To scale this idea to large 3D meshes, we introduce a local neighbourhood tokeniser that represents high-resolution velocity fields as compact spatial latent tokens and train latent flow-matching and masked-autoencoder models on these tokens. On simulations of intracranial aneurysm flow, our method reconstructs full velocity fields from sparse boundary context, outperforms supervised neural surrogates under boundary-condition and dataset shift and enables local geometry editing by reusing unchanged simulation context. These results suggest that viewing CFD inference as context-conditioned inpainting can turn neural surrogates from task-specific predictors into reusable flow priors. Code and demo are available at https://inpainting-physics.com.
♻ ☆ TopoPilot: Reliable Conversational Workflow Automation for Topological Data Analysis and Visualization
Nathaniel Gorski, Shusen Liu, Bei Wang
Recent agentic systems demonstrate that large language models can generate complex codebases from natural language prompts. Despite this progress, they present reliability concerns for scientific visualization due to invalid operations, subtle errors, and failure to resolve underspecified inputs. In this work, we introduce TopoPilot, a reliable and extensible agentic framework for automating complex scientific visualization workflows. We focus on topological data analysis and visualization as a primary use case, while designing the framework to generalize to broader visualization domains. TopoPilot employs a two-agent architecture: an orchestrator translates user prompts into workflows composed of atomic backend actions, while a verifier evaluates workflows prior to execution. Its modular design isolates components and supports new topological descriptors and domain-specific workflows without modifying the core system. It also employs numerous deterministic guardrails to ensure semantic consistency and accurate execution. To systematically improve reliability, we develop a taxonomy of failure modes and employ targeted safeguards for each class of error. Across 2,000 simulated multi-turn conversations spanning 100 prompts, including adversarial and infeasible requests, TopoPilot achieves a success rate exceeding 95%, compared with under 50% for a baseline without comprehensive guardrails and verification. We also show that TopoPilot outperforms Claude Code and Codex on similar prompts in terms of accuracy, completion time, and token usage.
comment: 21 pages, 10 figures
♻ ☆ gHAWK: Structural Encoding for Scalable Training of Graph Neural Networks on Knowledge Graphs NeurIPS 2026
Humera Sabir, Fatima Farooq, Ashraf Aboulnaga
Knowledge Graphs (KGs) are a rich source of structured data, and graph neural networks (GNNs) are the dominant tool for learning over them. However, existing message-passing GNNs struggle to scale to large KGs because they rely on the iterative message passing process to learn graph structure. This process is inefficient, especially under mini-batch training, where a node sees only a partial view of its neighborhood. In this paper, we address this problem and present gHAWK, a novel and scalable GNN training framework for large KGs. The key idea is to precompute structural features for each node that capture its local and global structure before GNN training even begins. Specifically, gHAWK introduces a preprocessing step that computes: (a) Bloom filters to compactly encode local neighborhood structure, and (b) TransE embeddings to represent each node's global position in the graph. These features are then fused with any domain-specific features (e.g., text embeddings), producing a node feature vector that can be used with any GNN backbone. Equipped with these structural priors, the GNN no longer needs to rediscover graph structure, significantly improving convergence and model accuracy with little memory overhead. Extensive experiments on large datasets from the Open Graph Benchmark demonstrate that gHAWK improves accuracy on both node property prediction and link prediction tasks. Remarkably, gHAWK enables simple GNNs to match or exceed more complex relation-aware ones, suggesting that careful preprocessing can substitute for architectural complexity in KG learning.
comment: Appears in NeurIPS 2026
♻ ☆ Computation, Not Memory: Chain-of-Thought and State Tracking in LLM Agents
Pedram Mouseli, Massieh Moayedi
Language-model agents often reason before they act, and the value of monitoring that reasoning depends on how it relates to their actions. We ask how an agent's actions depend on its reasoning when the correct action depends on a changing state. In a small file-system task, background events announce which file's lock has been toggled but not its new value. The agent therefore has to reconstruct the current locks from its history before it can move files safely. With Qwen3-8B and Qwen3.5-9B, we separate two roles of reasoning: generating it before each action, and retaining earlier reasoning in the prompt. Most of the reduction in lock-violating commands comes from reasoning written at the moment of action. Retaining earlier reasoning adds little when the agent also reasons at each step, but it helps an agent that does not reason, and it helps in longer episodes. Retained notes have a limit: when a later event makes a note wrong, an agent without current reasoning responds little, while current reasoning makes the action follow the event. The benefit depends on what the reasoning says. Filler text, reasoning written for another history and an accurate table of the state do not reproduce it. When we give the agent reasoning written for a history that differs in one lock value, the agent acts on that reasoning even against its own history. For Qwen3-8B, this holds also when that value has since been toggled. Without reasoning, state readouts are less reliable after toggles, and Qwen3-8B's answers about the state favor the outdated value. The state answer and the action also depend on different parts of the prompt. In this setting, the benefit of reasoning for rule-following comes mainly from generating it at each step, where it makes the action respond to later events. The state that can be read out without reasoning is a limited guide to how the agent acts.
comment: v2: adds retention without current reasoning and in longer episodes, tests of retained notes and current reasoning after a state change, explicit event labels, counterfactual pairs with a toggled lock, and readouts on outdated values
♻ ☆ A Multi-Center Dataset and Benchmark for SYNTAX Segmentation of Coronary Angiograms WACV 2027
Dominik Bernard Lau, Jerzy Szyjut, Hubert Malinowski, Adam Brzeski, Tomasz Dziubich, Natalia Zielińska, Tomasz Figatowski, Radosław Targoński
Dense pixel-level classification of coronary angiography is essential for automated cardiovascular diagnostics, yet the computer vision community lacks gold-standard protocols and robust datasets to tackle this topologically complex, heavily long-tailed domain. To bridge this gap, we introduce CARDIAG: a rigorous, multi-center benchmark dataset designed to evaluate deep learning architectures on fine-grained SYNTAX segment classification. Unlike prior efforts, CARDIAG systematically prevents patient- and center-level data leakage while providing an unprecedented suite of annotations: highly imbalanced multi-class labels, explicit catheter and stenosis masks, expert uncertainty maps, temporal sequence frames, and spatial metadata. Using CARDIAG, we conduct the most extensive architectural sweep in this domain, benchmarking 24 models spanning classic CNNs, Vision Transformers (ViTs), and State-Space Models (SSMs). Moving beyond naive overlap metrics, we evaluate topological preservation (clDice), vessel diameter error, and uncertainty error-detection. Our analysis reveals an insight: modern large-kernel CNNs (particularly ConvNeXt V2 with DeepLabV3+) still outperform recent ViTs and SSMs under a shared training recipe, establishing a Dice = 0.456. By ensembling complementary models, we push the baseline to Dice = 0.479. Through leave-one-center-out cross-validation and data efficiency analyses, we explore the current limits of out-of-distribution generalization. Ultimately, CARDIAG establishes a foundation for advancing medical computer vision for cardiology across many downstream tasks, including lesion detection, temporal frame interpolation, and 3D reconstruction.
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027 Dataset available on Zenodo at https://zenodo.org/records/19958730, code available at https://github.com/cvlab-ai/cardiag-benchmark
♻ ☆ When Do Rankings Beat Signs? Gradient Direction Recovery under Even Nuisance
Zhuangzhuang Pan, Yan Xia, Chee Seng Chan
Comparison-based optimization minimizes an objective using only ordinal feedback without numerical values. Sign-based baselines evaluate symmetric perturbation pairs in isolation, retaining only within-pair signs and discarding cross-pair orders from the same ranked batch. We ask when complete batch rankings provably beat within-pair signs under an unknown differentiable even nuisance, such as quadratic curvature. We show that reversed cross-pair comparisons cancel shared nuisance offsets without estimating a Hessian, and introduce a geometric framework characterizing three nested direction sets, namely Mirror, Reverse, and Full. Rather than curvature magnitude or condition number, we identify relative shell variation $τ_a$, the nuisance range on a radius-$a$ sphere divided by $a\|g\|$ for gradient $g\ne 0$ in $d$ dimensions, as a key quantity governing localization. For target angular accuracy $\varepsilon$ in radians, whenever $τ_a\le c\varepsilon/\sqrt{d}$ for a small absolute constant $c$, one-round Reverse constraints from uniform directions localize every surviving direction within angle $\varepsilon$ of the gradient using $\widetilde{O}(d+\sqrt{d/\varepsilon})$ evaluations, versus $Θ(d/\varepsilon)$ for signs. This whole-cell guarantee needs no variation bound as input and matches a lower bound up to log factors. Conversely, over well-conditioned quadratics with unbounded curvature relative to gradient scale, rankings offer no minimax evaluation advantage over signs, even across multiple rounds. Experiments certify strict Full-over-Reverse separation, and on two ridge tasks under joint evaluation and round caps, although Full shows no established gain beyond reversed constraints, Reverse consistently attains lower terminal gaps than tuned Mirror and unit-normalized ZO-RankSGD.
comment: This paper proves how black-box optimizers can reuse discarded batch rankings to cancel unknown curvature and recover accurate search directions with far fewer queries. (13 main pages; full proofs and experimental details in the appendices
♻ ☆ On the Global Convergence of Gradient Descent for multi-layer ResNets in the mean-field regime
Zhiyan Ding, Shi Chen, Qin Li, Stephen Wright
Finding the optimal configuration of parameters in ResNet is a nonconvex minimization problem, but first-order methods often find the global optimum when the network is overparameterized and the training algorithm is run for sufficiently many iterations. We study this phenomenon in the mean-field regime, where the network can be described approximately by an ordinary integral equation (OIE) and the training process of ResNet becomes a gradient-flow partial differential equation (PDE). Under the condition that the activation function is $2$-homogeneous or partially $1$-homogeneous, we show that this gradient-flow PDE converges to the global minimum. This result suggests that if the ResNet is sufficiently large, first-order optimization methods can find global minimizers that fit the training data as well. Further, by controlling the generalization error, we prove that the gradient-flow PDE is stable with respect to its cost function, implying that a finite-sized but sufficiently large dataset drawn from the underlying data distribution can exhibit the properties of the continuous limit. We give lower bounds on the depth and width of the network for the gradient-flow approximation to hold. We also lower-bound the size of the training data set needed to attain accurate approximation.
♻ ☆ TabularMath: Evaluating Computational Extrapolation in Tabular Learning via Program-Verified Synthesis ICML 2026
Zerui Cheng, Jiashuo Liu, Jianzhu Yao, Pramod Viswanath, Ge Zhang, Wenhao Huang
Standard tabular benchmarks reward interpolation: predicting values inside the data manifold, where local statistical smoothing works. However, much high-value tabular data, from pricing and financial rules to physical simulation, is produced by deterministic computations rather than noisy relationships. Can tabular models move from statistical interpolation to computational extrapolation, returning exact answers even beyond the range seen in training? We introduce TabularMath, a benchmark of 114 deterministic computations (233,472 rows) compiled from GSM8K and AIME problems into verified programs. We evaluate nine tabular methods, closed-form and symbolic regression baselines, and in-context learning with GPT-OSS-120B. On regression metrics, TabPFN v2.5 looks excellent: with 128 rows its median $R^2$ is 0.999 in-distribution, and it is the only tabular method whose median $R^2$ stays positive (0.76) when nearly every answer exceeds the training range. Exact answers tell a different story. Out of distribution (OOD), its accuracy falls from 39.5% to 7.8%, it answers no query correctly in 70 of 100 GSM8K tasks, and sixteen times more rows raise its OOD accuracy by only 0.4 points. Yet the answers are in the table: by construction, every label is a program's output on the row's inputs, and the training rows typically suffice to recover that program. Symbolic regression on the numbers alone recovers every OOD answer in 72 of 100 GSM8K tasks, and in-context learning with GPT-OSS-120B answers 39.2% of OOD queries. Tabular foundation models fit the trend but miss the computation, an inductive-bias gap that more data does not close. The competition-level AIME tasks remain open for every method.
comment: 31 pages, 7 figures, 22 tables. Final version. A preliminary version appeared at the ICML 2026 AI4Math Workshop
♻ ☆ Disentangling Self-Distillation: Measuring and Modeling Acquisition and Retention
Luis Zuin, Alexis Huet, Dario Rossi, Zied Ben Houidi
Self-distillation with privileged context adapts a language model from demonstrations by letting the model, once conditioned on a reference response, teach its context-free copy token by token. Our taxonomy reveals existing methods differ along three entangled axes: (i) the rollout source (student or teacher), (ii) the teacher coupling (frozen, or an exponential moving average of the student at some coupling rate) and (iii) the token-level divergence (here, reverse or forward KL), yet these axes are usually studied in fixed combinations and have led to conflicting conclusions. We formalize a unifying framework that covers both self-distillation and classic supervised fine-tuning: we train every combination of the three axes, on Qwen2.5-7B and Ministral-3-3B across ordinary and contradictory tasks, totaling 1,200 adaptation runs, to systematically investigate the impact of the above axes. We propose a controlled model of the same objective to interpret the resulting acquisition-retention trade-offs. We find that (i) the rollout source matters mostly where the task contradicts the pretrained behavior: there teacher rollouts raise acquisition (the accuracy gained on the new task) well above what student rollouts achieve, with almost no change in retention (the change in accuracy on general benchmarks); (ii) the teacher coupling changes acquisition most, on every task: acquisition rises with the coupling rate, then falls past a task-specific rate; (iii) switching the KL direction costs retention in one model but not the other, so which axis to tune first depends on the model. The controlled model reproduces the three trends.
♻ ☆ Chain of Operators: An Inference-Time Harness for In-Context Operator Learning
Minghui Yang, Chenghan Wu, Ling Guo, Liu Yang
While scientific foundation models show immense promise in accelerating physical simulations and numerical forecasting, they remain notoriously brittle when encountering out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. Adapting these generalist models to complex OOD tasks typically requires expensive parameter fine-tuning. In linguistic AI, this bottleneck is bypassed using "harnesses", which serve as external scaffolding such as reasoning chains and tool use to adapt frozen weights to complex tasks, yet designing an equivalent harness for physical domains remains an open frontier. To bridge this gap, we introduce Chain of Operators (CHOP), a framework that guides a frozen foundation model through complex OOD tasks without updating a single weight. By exploiting the in-context learning capability of In-Context Operator Networks (ICON), CHOP systematically decomposes unfamiliar problems into a sequence of explicit, closed-form mathematical operations and multiple model calls, translating OOD queries back into the model's learned operating regime. Across diverse benchmarks, including canonical PDE problems and real-world air-quality forecasting, CHOP consistently and substantially reduces inference errors compared to direct model evaluation. Crucially, these modular operator chains remain fully interpretable and can generalize across entirely distinct families of physical equations. Ultimately, this work demonstrates how frozen scientific models can adapt through programmable inference, establishing a modular, potential paradigm for agentic scientific computing.
♻ ☆ Fast Training of Mixture-of-Experts for Time Series Forecasting via Expert Loss Integration
Btissame El Mahtout, Florian Ziel
We propose a novel Mixture-of-Experts framework, referred to as Expert Loss Integration MoE (EliMoE), for time series forecasting. EliMoE addresses the optimization problem arising from small gating weights by incorporating expert-specific losses, which provide each expert with a direct learning signal independent of the gate-assigned weight. Specifically, the overall objective comprises the base forecasting loss and expert-specific losses, allowing individual expert prediction errors to directly influence parameter updates alongside the aggregate forecasting error. The framework also encourages different experts to learn from different temporal segments of the data. The proposed framework is further combined with a partial online learning strategy that enables efficient incremental updates of model parameters. By integrating expert-level loss information with partial online learning, EliMoE improves forecasting performance while retaining computational efficiency. Empirical results across five benchmark datasets from diverse application domains with different sampling frequencies show that the proposed approach generally outperforms state-of-the-art supervised neural forecasting models, including Transformer-based architectures such as PatchTST, as well as zero-shot time-series foundation models such as TimeMoE. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the expert-specific loss integration strategy, highlighting its contribution to enhancing predictive performance.
♻ ☆ Poisson-GENERIC Neural Operators: Exact Metriplectic Structure in Function Space via Casimir Entropies
Jason Sulskis, Sathya Ravi
Existing thermodynamically consistent neural operators enforce GENERIC degeneracy by projecting the reversible operator, introducing state dependence and generally forfeiting the Jacobi identity. We instead use the compatible Lie--Poisson pencil $L=αD+λ(uD+Du)$ for nonlinear transport and constant Poisson multipliers otherwise. Augmenting $u$ with a latent entropy density $s$ makes $S=\int s$ a Casimir, so $L\,δS/δz=0$ without projection. The energy combines a fixed mechanical quadratic, a learned gauge-free potential, and a convex internal energy; the friction operator $M=AA^{\!\top}$ enforces $M\,δE/δz=0$ pointwise and supports diffusion and damping through local Onsager fluxes. Skewness, positivity, and both degeneracies hold algebraically for any parameters; the continuum pencil satisfies Jacobi, with discrete residuals at machine precision on alias-free inputs. Closed-form heat and damped-wave friction operators are exactly representable, and a discrete-gradient integrator preserves the first and second laws. Across four PDEs in one and two dimensions and three backbones (FNO, Transolver, CNO), the model wins $62/72$ seed-level comparisons against unconstrained baselines at equal optimizer steps, recovers exact transport and wave symbols, matches heat and Burgers dissipation within $12\%$, and dissipates nothing on advection. At equal wall-clock time, the unconstrained FNO is more accurate over ten frames. Over one hundred frames, in and out of distribution, our model never increases physical energy and conserves it when dissipation vanishes, whereas the unconstrained FNO loses a quarter of conserved energy out of distribution and projected GENERIC-FNO often creates energy. Limitations include late-time heat under-damping and explicit-integrator divergence on waves.
comment: Preprint. Under Review
♻ ☆ AECSF: Adaptive Ensemble Conditional Score Filtering for High-Dimensional Nonlinear Data Assimilation
Yangwen Zhang, Shiwei Ni, Xiaoping Zhang, Xiaofei Guan, Lili Ju
In high-dimensional filters, particle weights can concentrate on a few members, while Gaussian updates can miss non-Gaussian posterior structure. A diffusion filter updates a forecast ensemble by gradually denoising particles in light of a new observation. Each noisy particle can correspond to several system states, and these states can have very different likelihoods. A score correction based on a single state can therefore misrepresent the posterior. We propose the Adaptive Ensemble Conditional Score Filter (AECSF), which uses the conditional Tweedie identity to express the required score through the mean state given the particle and the observation. All reverse particles share a set of proposals, but each assigns its own weights to estimate its conditional mean. As denoising proceeds, the reverse particles guide which proposals are resampled. We characterize when fixed proposals yield the exact noisy posterior score and bound the contribution of conditional-mean errors to the final sampling error. In controlled Gaussian experiments, AECSF samples the posterior more accurately than the tested likelihood-guidance rules. With 20 forecast members in 10,000-dimensional Lorenz-96, AECSF has lower RMSE and CRPS than the tested tempered SMC and kernel-density filters. On Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, the analysis ensembles also improve subsequent forecasts over the tested baselines at comparable cost. For Navier-Stokes flow, we learn a forecast prior that captures spatial dependence in vorticity and use it to reconstruct the full field from sparse velocity measurements.
♻ ☆ Object-Centric World Models for Causality-Aware Reinforcement Learning AAAI-26
Yosuke Nishimoto, Takashi Matsubara
World models have been developed to support sample-efficient deep reinforcement learning agents. However, it remains challenging for world models to accurately replicate environments that are high-dimensional, non-stationary, and composed of multiple objects with rich interactions since most world models learn holistic representations of all environmental components. By contrast, humans perceive the environment by decomposing it into discrete objects, facilitating efficient decision-making. Motivated by this insight, we propose \emph{Slot Transformer Imagination with CAusality-aware reinforcement learning} (STICA), a unified framework in which object-centric Transformers serve as the world model and causality-aware policy and value networks. STICA represents each observation as a set of object-centric tokens, together with tokens for the agent action and the resulting reward, enabling the world model to predict token-level dynamics and interactions. The policy and value networks then estimate token-level cause--effect relations and use them in the attention layers, yielding causality-guided decision-making. Experiments on object-rich benchmarks demonstrate that STICA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art agents in both sample efficiency and final performance.
comment: Accepted by AAAI-26. Code is available at https://github.com/nishimoto0430/STICA. v4: Fixed the mean score of STICA in Table 1 and the hyperparameters in Table 3. Updated Figure 7
♻ ☆ Differentially Private Manifold Denoising
Jiaqi Wu, Yiqing Sun, Zhigang Yao
Modern data analysis increasingly relies on manifold-based methods that use local geometry to extract low-dimensional structure from noisy observations. Yet in domains such as biomedicine and public health, privacy regulations restrict access to individual-level data, while perturbations introduced to protect privacy can distort the geometric information needed for analysis. We introduce a manifold denoising framework that uses private reference data to correct noisy public queries, bringing differential privacy to local geometric estimation. Starting from a hard correction based on the estimated tangent space, we develop a noise-adaptive soft correction that avoids specifying the intrinsic dimension. Furthermore, we construct a shared Gaussian field that couples evaluations across locations and bandwidths with moderate marginal noise inflation. Under standard assumptions on manifold regularity and sampling density, we establish non-asymptotic utility guarantees that characterize how denoising accuracy depends on sample size, noise level, bandwidth, and the privacy budget. Simulations and UK Biobank applications demonstrate accurate signal recovery under moderate privacy budgets. These results illustrate clear utility--privacy trade-offs and provide a practical DP component for manifold-based workflows in regulated environments.
comment: 76 pages
♻ ☆ Does This Gradient Spark Joy?
Ian Osband
Policy gradient computes a backward pass for every sample, although the backward pass is expensive and most samples carry little learning value. The Delightful Policy Gradient (DG) scores learning value in the forward pass with \emph{delight}, the product of advantage and surprisal (negative log-probability). We introduce the \emph{Kondo gate}, which compares delight against a compute price and pays for a backward pass only when the sample is worth it; sweeping the price traces a quality--cost trade-off. On MNIST, keeping 3\% of gradient terms learns faster than standard policy gradient even when backward passes are free, and nearly matches full DG. In bandits, zero-price gating preserves the expected gradient direction and removes its perpendicular noise, delight ranks samples more reliably than additive mixes of value and surprise, and a rare action with high reward variance marks where delight fails. On transformer token reversal, the gate's advantage grows with sequence length and vocabulary size. Because delight tolerates moderate noise, a cheap approximate forward pass could screen samples before expensive backpropagation, a training analogue of speculative decoding.
♻ ☆ Delightful Policy Gradient under Distributed Friction
Ian Osband
Distributed reinforcement learning trains on data from stale, buggy, or mismatched actors, whose actions often have high surprisal (negative log-probability) under the learner's policy. Supervised fine-tuning learns stably from such logged data, while policy gradient often does not. We trace the difference to negative learning from surprising data: rare failures can dominate finite-batch updates, while rare successes carry information the current policy would otherwise miss. The Delightful Policy Gradient (DG) separates the two by gating each term with delight, the product of advantage and surprisal, and needs no behavior probabilities. In a contaminated bandit, DG suppresses the perpendicular noise of rare failures by a factor that vanishes as the learner improves; no gate based only on learner probability can do this without also suppressing rare successes. On MNIST with stale actors, DG beats importance-weighted policy gradient given the exact behavior probabilities. On a transformer sequence task, DG often reaches an order of magnitude lower error under staleness, actor--learner probability mismatch, actor bugs, reward corruption, and rare discovery. With four frictions combined, its sample-efficiency advantage grows with sequence length. All experiments are controlled diagnostics; we do not evaluate an end-to-end distributed system.
♻ ★ On the interplay between noise and curvature and its effect on optimization and generalization AISTATS 2020
Valentin Thomas, Fabian Pedregosa, Bart van Merriënboer, Pierre-Antoine Manzagol, Yoshua Bengio, Nicolas Le Roux
The speed at which one can minimize an expected loss using stochastic methods depends on two properties: the curvature of the loss and the variance of the gradients. While most previous works focus on one or the other of these properties, we explore how their interaction affects optimization speed. Further, as the ultimate goal is good generalization performance, we clarify how both curvature and noise are relevant to properly estimate the generalization gap. Realizing that the limitations of some existing works stems from a confusion between these matrices, we also clarify the distinction between the Fisher matrix, the Hessian, and the covariance matrix of the gradients.
comment: Accepted to AISTATS 2020
♻ ☆ FreshRetailNet-50K: A Stockout-Annotated Censored Demand Dataset for Latent Demand Recovery and Forecasting in Fresh Retail
Yangyang Wang, Jiawei Gu, Li Long, Xin Li, Li Shen, Zhouyu Fu, Xiangjun Zhou, Xu Jiang
Accurate demand estimation is critical for the retail business in guiding the inventory and pricing policies of perishable products. However, it faces fundamental challenges from censored sales data during stockouts, where unobserved demand creates systemic policy biases. Existing datasets lack the temporal resolution and annotations needed to address this censoring effect. To fill this gap, we present FreshRetailNet-50K, the first large-scale benchmark for censored demand estimation. It comprises 50,000 store-product time series of detailed hourly sales data from 898 stores in 18 major cities, encompassing 863 perishable SKUs meticulously annotated for stockout events. The hourly stock status records unique to this dataset, combined with rich contextual covariates, including promotional discounts, precipitation, and temporal features, enable innovative research beyond existing solutions. We demonstrate one such use case of two-stage demand modeling: first, we reconstruct the latent demand during stockouts using precise hourly annotations. We then leverage the recovered demand to train robust demand forecasting models in the second stage. Experimental results show that this approach achieves a 2.73% improvement in prediction accuracy while reducing the systematic demand underestimation from 7.37% to near-zero bias. With unprecedented temporal granularity and comprehensive real-world information, FreshRetailNet-50K opens new research directions in demand imputation, perishable inventory optimization, and causal retail analytics. The unique annotation quality and scale of the dataset address long-standing limitations in retail AI, providing immediate solutions and a platform for future methodological innovation. The data (https://huggingface.co/datasets/Dingdong-Inc/FreshRetailNet-50K) and code (https://github.com/Dingdong-Inc/frn-50k-baseline}) are openly released.
♻ ☆ SLA-Aware Task Offloading in the IoT Edge-Cloud Continuum: Class-Weighted Deep Reinforcement Learning Against an Exact Optimum
Shilpa Golla, Tharun Kumar Korine Palli, Urmila Bandaru
Deep reinforcement learning (RL) is often used to decide where Internet of Things (IoT) tasks with different latency limits run in the edge-cloud continuum, yet some methods give every missed task the same penalty and few compare their agents with an optimal policy. This benchmark study builds four offloading systems small enough to solve exactly by dynamic programming and measures reward and learner against the optimum. A bonus for a met limit makes each miss cost its penalty plus the bonus, which shifts the class weights of published per-class rewards. A class-blind penalty stays 65% to 118% above the optimal cost even with a perfect learner, while a corrected per-class penalty comes within 0.13% of the optimum. With a per-class reward, tuned proximal policy optimization (PPO) agents come within 9% to 11% of the optimum in the smallest system, and the corrected one beats a tuned reservation rule in 9 of 10 seeds. In larger systems the agents stay 41% to 76% above the optimum, and a tuned rule beats their mean. Training ten times longer does not close this gap, and a PPO-Lagrangian agent with reachable targets does no better than the per-class reward.
♻ ☆ Does Learning Order Explain Forgetting? The Lie Bracket as an Early-Warning Signal for Catastrophic Forgetting Without Old Data
Ephraim Kofi Ayi Kwapong
A network trained on task A and then task B ends at different weights than one trained on B and then A. To leading order this gap is set by the Lie bracket of the two tasks' gradient fields, and Dherin (2023) conjectured that a non-vanishing bracket may be linked to catastrophic forgetting. I test this conjecture empirically. Across Split MNIST, Split Fashion-MNIST and Split CIFAR-10, the forgetting of A is almost exactly the difference in A's loss between the two training orders (Spearman rho = 0.96-1.00). I then ask whether the bracket can predict that forgetting early in training on B and without any of A's data, using only a small summary stored when A finishes: its gradient and its top 20 Hessian eigenpairs. When the old task is well learned and forgetting is slow (task-incremental), this stored bracket ranks forgetting with rho = 0.70-0.81, against 0.33-0.58 for the penalty of Elastic Weight Consolidation, and matches or exceeds re-evaluating A on its own data. When forgetting is fast (domain-incremental), the stored summary goes stale and the EWC penalty is as good or better. The bracket fails outright when the old task is only half learned; I trace this to a residual gradient on A an order of magnitude larger, which makes first-order (slope) damage matter. In five-task sequences with slow forgetting, the stored bracket outperforms the EWC penalty on MNIST and CIFAR-10 features (by 0.16-0.17) and ties it on Fashion-MNIST; it fades as summaries age on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, where a Taylor estimate from the same summary holds up better. The bracket is therefore a useful early-warning signal for the quiet kind of forgetting, under a clear condition, provided the summary is kept fresh.
comment: v2: adds five-task sequence experiments (Section 5.5, Appendix G) and related work. 17 pages, 6 figures. Code and results: https://github.com/Hackme262/lie-bracket-forgetting
♻ ☆ Reinforcement Learning Under Runtime Confounding: Policy Learning and Off-Policy Evaluation
Raphael Kim, Michele Santacatterina, Ramin Zabih, Keith Barnatchez
Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used to train robust, adaptable systems across healthcare, e-commerce, and robotics. In these settings, legal, ethical, or logistical concerns may preclude certain key variables that drive decisions from being collected during deployment time. This gives rise to a setting known as runtime confounding: the logged data hold full observability, but deployment time lacks knowledge of certain variables, known as runtime confounders. Unlike single timepoint and non-adaptive settings, runtime confounding under reinforcement learning has the potential to propagate over time, as earlier decisions affect future states, observations, and action assignments, leading to biased learning. We address these problems with three contributions: we (1) develop policy learning algorithms under runtime-confounding, (2) develop semi-parametric efficient off-policy estimation procedures, and (3) provide diagnostics for understanding the price of runtime confounding.
♻ ☆ EssentialGIN: a new approach for gene essentiality prediction based on graph isomorphism neural networks
Sahar Mansourirad, Zahra Narimani, Parvin Razzaghi, Nazanin Hosseinkhan
Background: Prediction of essential genes (proteins), is a basic and challenging problem but at the same time very costly and time-consuming in wet-lab experiments. Predicting essential genes, only based on computational methods (to introduce wet-lab candidates) using centrality measures are not accurate and result in large number of false positives; therefore, more complex models such as deep learning and also integration of biological information are used in recent research to identify essential genes. Methods: In this work we focus on graph isomorphism networks, in order to embed proteins as a node in PPI network to conserve topological features of PPI network, and also integrate biological data such as gene expression data, gene orthology information and gene subcellular localization information, and introduced a deep architecture for predicting essential genes. Graph isomorphism network architecture is modified in this work for embedding node information. Results: Our experiments proved that the proposed method outperforms baseline centrality-based methods and also machine learning based methods such as Node2Vec, MLP, and also graph attention networks (GAT). Conclusion: In this paper we observed that using graph isomorphism networks that integrate biological data (as node attributes) and preserve network topology can significantly improve the essential gene prediction accuracy. In simpler organisms such as E. coli and D. melanogaster, methods such as multi-layer perceptron using Node2Vec embedding also performs very good, but in H. sapiens the introduced architecture significantly outperforms deep learning and other graph neural network solutions. Keywords: Essential gene prediction, graph neural network, graph isomorphism network, PPI network, node embedding

♻ ☆ Trust Region Q Adjoint Matching NeurIPS 2026
Yonghoon Dong, Kyungmin Lee, Changyeon Kim, Jaehyuk Kim, Jinwoo Shin
Off-policy reinforcement learning of pretrained flow policies remains challenging due to the instability of optimization arising from the multi-step sampling process. Recently, Q-learning with Adjoint Matching (QAM) addressed this by recasting policy improvement as a stochastic optimal control (SOC) problem guided by a learned critic. However, QAM inherits a fundamental fragility of critic-guided improvement, since small critic errors can be exponentially amplified and often lead to performance collapse. This paper introduces Trust Region Q Adjoint Matching (TRQAM), a stable off-policy fine-tuning algorithm that adaptively controls the path-space KL between the fine-tuned and pretrained policies through projected dual descent. Specifically, we adapt a trust-region parameter $λ$ inside the sampling process of the flow policy and prove that $λ$ exactly weights the path-space KL in the SOC objective. As a result, our method can tightly control the deviation from the pretrained policy within a prescribed KL budget, achieving stable off-policy RL. Through experiments on 50 OGBench tasks, TRQAM consistently outperforms prior methods in both offline RL and offline-to-online RL. In particular, TRQAM achieves an overall success rate of 68% in offline RL, substantially improving over the strongest baseline at 46%.

♻ ☆ Uncertainty-Aware Hybrid Offline Reinforcement Learning with Online Action Selection Enabled by Sparse Gaussian-Process Critics
Marco Chan, Christos Evripidou, Liqiu Dong, Benoit Chachuat, Mehmet Mercangöz
Start-ups and grade changes remain largely operator-driven, while developing and maintaining dynamic models for model-based control requires substantial engineering effort. Hybrid Offline Learning and Online Optimisation (HOFLON) uses one-step offline reinforcement learning to select actions from historical transition data. In its original implementation, the online objective combines the predicted return from a tree-ensemble critic with an adversarial-autoencoder (AAE) penalty for unfamiliar state-action pairs. We examine the effect of this penalty and replace the critic and AAE with a sparse variational Gaussian-process (sGP) critic. Actions maximise $μ- κσ$, an uncertainty-adjusted estimate of the return from one action followed by the historical operating practice. On the HOFLON polymerisation-reactor benchmark, removing the AAE from HOFLON led to 4 failed start-ups in 15 runs over five critics. At its published weight, the variation in the AAE penalty is four orders of magnitude smaller than the variation in the tree-ensemble critic. Nevertheless, it changes actions when the predicted returns of competing candidates are nearly equal, and paired runs with and without the penalty diverged from the first move. With a Matérn-5/2 sGP critic, $κ= 0$ led to failure in 13 of 15 runs, whereas with $κ= 3$ none of 15 runs (five critics, three noise realisations) failed. The median and lowest returns were 13,464 and 13,398 (HOFLON: 13,393 and 12,411). A squared-exponential sGP critic with learned inducing inputs needed $κ\geq 3$ to remain within the empirical data support in steady state, and then settled with a temperature offset of 2.0 K.

♻ ☆ Quadratic Gradient: Accelerating Privacy-Preserving Logistic Regression Training with Homomorphic Encryption
John Chiang
Training logistic regression over encrypted data has emerged as a prominent approach to addressing security concerns in recent years. In this paper, we introduce an efficient gradient variant, termed the \textit{quadratic gradient}, which is specifically designed for privacy-preserving logistic regression while remaining equally effective in plaintext optimization. By incorporating this quadratic gradient, we enhance Nesterov's Accelerated Gradient (NAG), Adaptive Gradient (AdaGrad), and Adam algorithms. We evaluate these enhanced algorithms across various datasets, with experimental results demonstrating state-of-the-art convergence rates that significantly outperform traditional first-order gradient methods. Furthermore, we apply the enhanced NAG method to implement homomorphic logistic regression training, achieving comparable performance within only four iterations. The proposed quadratic-gradient approach offers a unified framework that synergizes the advantages of first-order gradient methods and second-order Newton-type methods, suggesting broad applicability to diverse numerical optimization tasks.
♻ ☆ OmniHarness: Harnessing Generalizable Visual Generation via Symbolic Policy Learning
Xu Xu, Jinxiu Liu, Zhangbo Qiao, Cheng Song, Jiaxing Lu, Xiangyu Zhang, Yubin Gu, Fangwei Ning, Yan Shi
Unified multimodal large language models and multi-agent systems have advanced visual generation. However, several limitations remain. (1) Experience acquisition is typically reactive, occurring only in response to downstream tasks. (2) Accumulated knowledge varies in relevance and reliability, making efficient and effective reuse challenging. To address these limitations, we introduce OmniHarness, a framework for generalizable visual generation via symbolic policy learning. Before downstream objectives are specified, self-directed inquiry autonomously generates and executes practice tasks, with selection guided by capability novelty and the current competence frontier. Verified workflows are abstracted into symbolic policies that encode experience for task families. Symbolic retrieval searches workflow metadata in stages rather than full parameterized workflows, using reliability tiers to prioritize reliable knowledge. Execution feedback updates these policies after each task, guiding subsequent retrieval and reuse while model parameters remain fixed. Experiments across six benchmarks demonstrate strong performance and generalizable visual generation capabilities. On ComfyBench's Creative tasks, OmniHarness achieves a 95.0% resolve rate, exceeding the strongest baseline by 27.5 percentage points.
♻ ☆ Stochastic Grouping Conformal Prediction for Effective Subgroup Reliability
Meihui Zhong, Wenxin Tai, Ting Zhong, Fan Zhou
Conformal prediction offers a distribution-free coverage guarantee, making it especially attractive for clinical applications. Standard conformal prediction, however, provides such guarantees only at the population level, and its prediction sets can exhibit coverage disparities across clinically important subgroups. A natural remedy is to calibrate within predefined groups. However, this can require access to sensitive subgroup attributes and is prone to a worst-group bottleneck: protecting the most difficult subgroup can inflate prediction sets for all, increasing cognitive burden on decision makers. To this end, we propose Stochastic Grouping Conformal Prediction (SGCP), a conformal framework for subgroup-reliable uncertainty quantification. It learns a stochastic grouping map that allows each sample to draw calibration information from others with similar calibration behavior, yielding a local score law that boosts reliability across subpopulations. We prove that SGCP retains the standard coverage guarantee. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show that it consistently reduces subgroup coverage gaps while achieving smaller or comparable prediction set sizes relative to existing baselines.
